news.title: Iran hasn't tried to repair nuclear facilities damaged in US strikes, UN nuclear chief says
news.text:
The head of the UN nuclear agency said Tuesday there has been no indication Iran has tried to repair or reconstruct its nuclear facilities damaged in US and Israeli military strikes this year or last year.

President Donald Trump has said one of the major reasons the U.S. went to war with Iran on Feb. 28 was to deny Tehran the ability to develop nuclear weapons, even as he has insisted that strikes the US carried out on Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 “obliterated” the country's atomic program.

During a UN Security Council meeting, International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi urged Iran to give inspectors access to all nuclear sites, including those damaged in the military attacks. The IAEA has not been able to verify the status of Iran's stockpile of near weapons-grade uranium since the U.S. bombed its sites last year.

However, Grossi said that “since June 2025, we have not identified any activity to repair or reconstruct any of the facilities damaged in the military attacks of 2025 and 2026."

Trump has consistently downplayed the economic impact of the Iran war, which has emerged as a liability for Republicans heading into next week's midterm elections, and has argued that higher fuel prices are worth paying to prevent a nuclear-armed Iran. The White House didn't immediately respond Tuesday evening to a request for comment on Grossi's remarks.

Iran maintains that its nuclear program is peaceful. However, the IAEA says the country has a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60% purity — a short, technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90%.

The UN meeting on Tuesday was called by Bahrain, Denmark, Latvia, France, the United Kingdom and United States after the IAEA referred Iran to the Security Council for failing to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations. Russia and China, allies of Iran, tried unsuccessfully to prevent the meeting.

Under those obligations, which are part of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, Iran is legally bound to declare all nuclear material and activities and allow IAEA inspectors to verify that none of it is being diverted from peaceful uses.

Iran's UN deputy ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi attacked the council for its silence after the US-Israeli attacks, denouncing their “wars of aggression against Iran” and accusing the US of committing war crimes against the Iranian people.

He never mentioned the IAEA's unanswered questions or the demand to return its inspectors. Instead, he asserted that “Israel possesses nuclear weapons, yet your concern is the absence of inspectors in Iran.” Israel has never confirmed that it possesses nuclear weapons.

US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz called Iran a “brutal dictatorship” and asked if the Iranian ambassador wanted to apologize to Bahrain's envoy, a council member, for attacking his country.

“We've heard tireless allegations against the United States, ” he said. “What we have not heard today is an explanation for Iran's continued failure to satisfy its safeguard obligations.”

The IAEA asked Iran for answers, Waltz said, and it would be smart for the Iranian representative to start providing some answers.

“Your lies are no good here,” he said.

Published on October 28, 2026
news.summary: During a UN Security Council meeting, International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi urged Iran to give inspectors access to all nuclear sites, including those damaged in the military attacks

news.title: US urges Gulf allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes after midterms, report says
news.text: The United States has urged several Arab Gulf countries to prepare for a short but intense military campaign against Iran following next week's U.S. midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday, citing people briefed on discussions between Washington and regional governments. According to the report, the messages, delivered through diplomatic and military channels, are among a growing number of indications that the United States and Israel are preparing for another round of large-scale military operations against Iran. U.S. President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on whether to launch an attack but is leaning toward a broad military operation after the midterms, the newspaper reported. Potential targets include Iranian critical infrastructure and nuclear facilities. The alternative remains a negotiated agreement with Tehran. Regional mediators continue diplomatic efforts to avert another confrontation, but those talks have yet to produce a breakthrough. The reported preparations include significant changes to the U.S. military posture in the Middle East. Officials familiar with the matter told the Journal that the U.S. military is moving a Patriot air defense system from Texas to the region to strengthen its defenses against potential Iranian missile attacks. American forces have also been relocated from bases considered vulnerable to attack as part of preparations for a possible escalation. According to several officials cited in the report, U.S. troops stationed in the region have replenished their ammunition supplies, while American bombers and fighter jets are being readied for potential strikes. An additional aircraft carrier strike group and a Marine Corps expeditionary force are expected to join the U.S. military buildup next month, the newspaper reported. They would augment an armada of roughly 20 warships already operating in the Middle East, although some of the incoming vessels could replace ships currently deployed in the region rather than increase the overall number. Netanyahu: 'This is not over' The Journal's report emerged around the same time that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed supporters early Wednesday following Israel's parliamentary election. Netanyahu's Likud party remained the largest in the Knesset, according to exit polls, although his right-wing political bloc appeared to have lost significant ground, leaving his ability to form a governing coalition uncertain. Netanyahu opened his election-night address by focusing on Iran, declaring that Israel's confrontation with the Islamic Republic was far from over. "We have brought the Iranian regime to the brink of collapse," Netanyahu said. "And yet I tell you, this is still not over. Because as long as this fanatical regime exists, a regime that has defined its very purpose as destroying our existence, it will try again to destroy us." "We have the power, together with our wonderful friend President Trump, to remove this threat once and for all," he added. Netanyahu's remarks came shortly after his main rival Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar party, called on him to resign, describing him as "a caretaker prime minister without a mandate or public trust." Eisenkot made the comments Tuesday night, before dramatic overnight revisions to the election exit polls altered the projected balance between the political blocs. His warning reflected concerns among opposition figures that Netanyahu could seek to escalate security tensions to complicate efforts to replace him or pressure rival parties into joining an emergency government. Addressing senior defense and security officials, Eisenkot urged them to resist any attempt to involve the security establishment in political maneuvering. "Stand firm against any attempt to challenge you," he said. He then directed a warning at Netanyahu: "Do not dare use Israel's security for your political purposes."
news.summary: Washington reportedly warns Gulf states to prepare for short, intense military campaign as US forces bolster missile defenses, reposition troops and ready aircraft for potential strikes; Trump yet to decide whether to attack, while Netanyahu vows to eliminate Iran's threat
news.author: Moran Azulay

news.title: Hackers target US election watchdog's filing system days before midterm polls: Report
news.text: NEW YORK: The US Federal Election Commission (FEC) was targeted by a hacker or hackers, disrupting its electronic filing system days before the November 3 midterm elections, Reuters reported in an exclusive report, citing an email seen by the news agency.The outage comes as political groups and super PACs spend record amounts in the final days of the election campaign, which will determine whether US President Donald Trump's Republican Party retains its majorities in Congress.In a statement, the FEC said its electronic filing system was offline, adding that its information technology staff were working to restore the service.An email sent by an FEC electronic filings officer to campaign compliance firms on Monday night (local time) said, "We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems. As a result, we've had to temporarily shut down our web-facing services," according to Reuters.The outage has prevented political organisations from filing mandatory 24-hour and 48-hour campaign spending reports, which provide information about spending on specific races. However, users could still search the FEC website for previously filed reports, Reuters reported.The FEC later said the issue had been identified and a fix was being implemented..The FEC tracks campaign spending by candidates and political committees but does not administer US elections. The disruption is therefore not expected to affect voters' ability to cast their ballots.The cyber incident comes as Trump has emphasised election integrity ahead of the November 3 polls, which will determine control of both chambers of Congress and influence his legislative agenda for the remainder of his term.Trump has said he would respect the midterm election results if the polls were conducted honestly, while warning that he could use his veto power if necessary."We'll figure a way. I have a strong veto. I hope that won't be the case, but if it is, that's happened before… I will -- if they're honest elections," Trump told reporters.Earlier, Trump announced a USD 1 million reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of individuals involved in voter fraud linked to previous elections or the upcoming 2026 midterms.In a post on Truth Social, Trump said, "Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid $1,000,000 upon the arrest and conviction of those who created the Fraud! Thank you for your attention to this matter."The November 3 elections will see all 435 seats in the House of Representatives contested, along with approximately one-third of the Senate seats. The results are expected to shape the balance of political power in Washington and determine the extent to which the administration can advance its policy priorities.According to a CBS News poll published on Sunday, Democrats are projected to win 229 seats in the House, potentially securing a majority, although Republicans retain a narrow path to holding control.The CBS News/YouGov survey, conducted among 2,355 US adults between October 21 and 23, found that inflation, rising prices and broader economic concerns remain central to voters' decisions. news.title: Trump set to loosen emission rules for oil and gas
news.text:
CORPUS CHRISTI: President Donald Trump is set to announce Tuesday a sweeping rollback of rules that stop oil and gas producers from emitting methane, a greenhouse gas super pollutant.

Trump will make the announcement at a rally in support of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running for Senate, a White House official said.

Texas is by far the country’s leading fossil fuel producing state.

An Environmental Protection Agency statement earlier this month said undoing regulations put in place by Republican Trump’s Democratic predecessor Joe Biden would result in $45 billion in cost savings, without offering a detailed breakdown of the figure.

“Americans must be able to afford to heat their homes in the winter and fill up their car and drive to work. They can’t do that when the people producing the energy are weighed down by unnecessary burdens,” said EPA administrator Lee Zeldin.

Methane, the main component of natural gas, is the second-largest cause of global warming behind carbon dioxide -- responsible for about a third, or 0.5C, of total planetary heating since the pre-industrial era.

A molecule of methane traps far more heat than carbon dioxide, but persists in the atmosphere for only seven to 12 years, whereas carbon dioxide can last for hundreds of years.

The changes take aim at rules to curb methane emissions from oil and gas operations. Emissions occur at every stage, from extracting gas held underground, to processing, transmission and distribution.

“Lee Zeldin’s EPA is giving oil and gas corporations exactly what they’ve long wanted: a toothless methane standard they can use to pretend they’re well-regulated, all while they continue to knowingly leak and flare dangerous amounts of the heat-trapping gas,” said Julia Kane, a researcher at oil and gas watchdog Fieldnotes.

The United States is the world’s leading emitter of methane from its oil and gas sector, followed by Russia, according to the International Energy Agency.

The new changes include proposing to kill off the “Super Emitter Program,” a provision that allows EPA-approved observers to report major leaks with a rate of over 100 kilograms (220 pounds) per hour.

Another will weaken regulation against so-called “marginal wells” that produce 15 barrels or less of oil equivalent a day.

Yet another will relax rules around the routine flaring of “associated gas.” In places like the Permian Basin where oil is the main product, the associated gas that comes up is considered a byproduct, with the cost of capture exceeding its market value, leading operators to often burn it off, or flare it.

Published in Dawn, October 28th, 2026

news.title: Crypto blitzes U.S. midterms with $176 million as it prepares for post-Trump era
news.text: NEW YORK - The crypto industry has spent roughly $176 million across more than 100 midterm races this election cycle, as part of a yearslong plan to build a bipartisan coalition of allies in Congress that can advance its interests long after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office.The $2.75 trillion industry, and the billionaires who built it, are aggressively spending to elect friendly candidates while targeting politicians they see as a threat, according to interviews with more than a half-dozen crypto political strategists and a Reuters review of the spending.While the industry’s recent spending blitz is known, its long-term plan to further its legislative agenda is less well-understood. The industry isn’t just looking for allies; it is trying to pick candidates who already have a chance of winning, and can help once they get to Congress, the strategists said.
news.summary: The $2.75 trillion industry is aggressively spending to elect friendly candidates while targeting politicians it sees as a threat.

news.title: Netanyahu and rival each claim mandate after tight Israel election
news.text: JERUSALEM: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and rival Gadi Eisenkot each vowed on Wednesday to form a government after both came up short in the first election since the October 7, 2023 attack traumatised the country.Voters turned out Tuesday in the highest numbers in decades to give their verdict on the divisive rule of Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister who has pushed the country sharply to the right and unleashed a wave of wars in response to the Hamas attack.Exit polls showed Eisenkot, a former military chief and political novice, and his opposition bloc neck and neck with Netanyahu's hard-right camp and both well away from the threshold for a majority in parliament.The strongest gains came from Arab Israeli parties whose voters turned out in soaring numbers against Netanyahu, who has relentlessly warned that the minority would dilute the Jewish nationalist direction in which he has taken Israel.Netanyahu, greeting cheering supporters at a Jerusalem convention centre after 3:00 am (0100 GMT), called for a "strong government of the right" and said that the "Jewish and Zionist majority must unite".The 77-year-old prime minister was unusually brief and did not directly claim victory.Instead, he listed leaders Israel has killed under his orders and again hinted that he was ready for a third bombing campaign against Iran alongside US President Donald Trump, his close ally."Israel has a unique opportunity with our partner President Trump to forever eliminate the existential threat of Iran," Netanyahu said.Eisenkot, speaking to his own supporters in Tel Aviv, issued a veiled warning to Netanyahu, who observers say could use a war to push for a unity government."Netanyahu, don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.Addressing Israel's security establishment, Eisenkot said that they served the state and not Netanyahu, calling him "a caretaker prime minister, without a mandate or the people’s trust"..Israeli exit polls suggest no clear winner with Eisenkot's bloc neck and neck with Netanyahu.Public has voted for change Eisenkot shares many of Netanyahu's views on security and has backed the Gaza offensive following October 7 that has reduced the territory to rubble.But Eisenkot has vowed to create a more inclusive atmosphere inside Israel and to rein in extremist settlers in the West Bank who have attacked Palestinians with virtual impunity.After turnout of nearly 78 percent, the highest since 1999, Eisenkot said it would be a mistake to hold a second election and vowed to work "swiftly" to form a government."The public has voted for change," Eisenkot said. "A worthy leader would accept the people's vote of no confidence and announce his retirement from political life today."The three mainstream Israeli television networks in exit polls gave the two blocs each around 51 seats -- well below the 61 needed to govern -- after initially giving an edge to the opposition.Israeli Arab lists were projected to win 17 to 18 seats, a sharp gain, with some Israeli Arab communities reporting near-universal turnout driven by outrage to often derogatory rhetoric against them by Netanyahu's far-right allies.Key Israeli Arab leader Mansour Abbas said he believed the right had "suffered a major loss" and was open to working with Eisenkot.But Eisenkot said during the campaign he would not govern with Israeli Arab lawmakers -- and Netanyahu again suggested that a government relying on Arab votes would lack legitimacy.Arab lawmakers could give Eisenkot support in parliamentary votes to maintain a minority government without joining a coalition. If not, Israel could head to new elections.Itamar Ben Gvir, a far-right firebrand who according to exit polls did not gain as much as many expected, warned Netanyahu against another option -- a unity government with Eisenkot."It would be a terrible mistake," said Ben Gvir, who champions the expulsion of Palestinians and would likely be excluded from any unity government.Hebrew University of Jerusalem political scientist Gideon Rahat said Ben Gvir had succeeded in mobilising votes -- of Israeli Arabs.But he said: "Even if Netanyahu lost, that doesn't mean Eisenkot won.".DivisiveThe election came as Israel looks increasingly isolated on the world stage, driven by the war in Iran and the military campaign in Gaza, soaring settlement construction and violence in the occupied West Bank.Netanyahu himself faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court over Gaza as well as domestic corruption charges that could land him in prison if he loses power.Eisenkot is a political novice whose mild manner is the antithesis of the smooth-talking incumbent.The son of working-class Moroccan Jewish immigrants, Eisenkot would be the first prime minister of Middle Eastern or North African descent.Before voting, the 66-year-old Eisenkot paid his respects privately at the grave of his son Gal, whose death fighting in Gaza has drawn empathy from many Israelis.Tens of thousands of Israelis are estimated to have flown in from abroad for an election seen as crucial for their country.Eilana Zisblit, 55, told AFP she had travelled back from Canada, where she has lived for almost 30 years, to vote for a centre-right party in Eisenkot's bloc."The country is going in a really, really bad direction. Both for Jews and Arabs living in the country, and for Jews living abroad," she said.The time to act is "now, or the country really won't survive anymore"..A look at the main issues in Israeli elections seen as a referendum on Netanyahu.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Israeli vote deadlocked with Netanyahu level with Opposition
news.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot are neck and neck in the first election since the 2023 Hamas attacks, setting up a tense period of negotiations over who will form the next government. 

Netanyahu’s religious right-wing alliance and Eisenkot’s bloc are both on track to secure 51 of Israel’s 120 parliamentary seats, according to two exit polls published after voting closed late Tuesday. A third had Netanyahu slightly ahead, having earlier said Eisenkot was leading. 

That would leave the contenders well short of a majority needed to become the country’s next leader, with both facing a difficult path to forming a ruling coalition without a second election. Votes are still being counted, however, and the final picture could yet change. Further complicating matters, Netanyahu’s Likud looks set to be the biggest single party, with Eisenkot’s Yashar in second place.

The two Israeli Arab parties, which have emerged as potential kingmakers, are forecast to win 18 seats, the exit polls showed, ahead of expectations. Both have said they’d support Eisenkot on some level, having rallied supporters to help oust Netanyahu and prevent a new term they believe would be existential. 

Voter turnout was close to record highs throughout the day, reaching almost 78% as of 10 p.m, according to the central elections committee.

Should Eisenkot, 66, succeed in becoming prime minister, it would mark a stunning defeat for Netanyahu, 77, who has dominated Israel’s politics for much of the past three decades and led the country through three years of near constant war. While the final outcome of the election remains uncertain, it’s clear that a significant portion of the support that propelled Netanyahu to power in 2022 has been eroded. 

Many Israelis blame him for failing to prevent, and subsequently take responsibility for, the 2023 Hamas assault on Israel that was the deadliest day in Israeli history. Netanyahu has since waged military campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and against Iran, which he insists have made the country safer. 

“The public has spoken — it has fired the Netanyahu government,” Yair Golan, leader of the leftist Democrats Party and part of Eisenkot’s bloc, said in a statement. “We represent an enormous constituency that has spent four years fighting in the streets,” he said. “We are ready to work with our partners, bridge differences and take responsibility.”

But with the makeup of a new government likely to take days or weeks to finalize, Netanyahu remains Israel’s prime minister. That would enable him to join US President Donald Trump in a renewed bombing campaign of Iran after the US midterms next week, as both have repeatedly threatened.

Trump had endorsed Netanyahu, saying the incumbent had what it takes to “finish the job” in the eight-month war with the Islamic Republic. 

Eisenkot pitched himself as a more modest alternative to Netanyahu, while still emphasizing a commitment to resolving Israel’s myriad security challenges. On Iran, he has said the country’s nuclear program must be curbed, militarily if necessary, but that regime change in Tehran is “not an achievable goal.” 

No party in Israel’s history has won an outright election majority, requiring often long periods of coalition negotiations. President Isaac Herzog will nominate the presumptive prime minister based on the vote count and party recommendations. 

Polling stations in parts of Tel Aviv were packed on Tuesday, with lines snaking through schools — where many of the booths have been set up — and spilling into streets. Some of the political parties set up stands blaring out music, and handed out balloons, sweets and stickers to voters and their children.

Beyond national security, voters cast ballots on a set of domestic issues — including whether to draft ultra-Orthodox young men into the army. The power of the Supreme Court and judicial system, which Netanyahu has sought to undermine, transparency and corruption are also on the agenda.

For Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, where violence by Jewish settlers on Arabs has soared since the Hamas incursion, the election is unlikely to lead to any immediate changes. Like Netanyahu, Eisenkot has ruled out a two-state solution, saying it would threaten Israel’s security, though he’s condemned the government for supporting Israelis who have attacked Palestinians. 

Published on October 28, 2026
news.summary: Netanyahu’s religious right-wing alliance and Eisenkot’s bloc are both on track to secure 51 of Israel’s 120 parliamentary seats, according to two exit polls published after voting closed late Tuesday. A third had Netanyahu slightly ahead, having earlier said Eisenkot was leading.

news.title: Cuba's foreign minister disrupts UNGA meeting in dramatic confrontion with US envoy
news.text: Digital Desk | United Nations, Oct 28 (IANS) In a drama at the General Assembly, Cuba's Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla charged up to the dais yelling to confront US Permanent Representative Mike Waltz, disrupting a meeting on Washington's sanctions against his country. Assembly President Khalilur Rahman pleaded for calm, asking the Cubans to go back to their seat and let Waltz speak on Tuesday, and briefly suspended the meeting. As Waltz was criticising the Havana government, the Cuban delegation thumped their desk and yelled. They left their seats and marched towards the dais, as he accused the Cuban elite of corruption, saying, "Havana would have you believe everything in Cuba has just disappeared. Well, we know, we know where it went". Rodriguez kept interrupting Waltz, demanding to speak on a point of order. Both of them got into a staring match, Waltz up from the black marble rostrum, and Rodriguez and his troops down in front of the podium. Rahman pleaded, "Please help me in conducting the business in a smooth manner, and you will have that right", to a point of order. Waltz shouted at Rodriguez, "Back away! This isn't Havana". Meanwhile, Rahman, like a teacher trying to keep order in an unruly classroom, said, "Please sit down. Sit down", before suspending the meeting. "I'm here to administer the rules of procedure in a fair manner, in an independent manner", he said. When the meeting resumed within minutes, Rodriguez raised his point of order, which was more of a response, that Waltz was "lying grossly" and "offending the dignity of the people and government of Cuba". When Waltz resumed his speech, he said that Rodriguez had tried to silence him in front of cameras and ambassadors, but "imagine what happens if you dare to speak out under the iron fist of this regime". He displayed photographs of what he said was a "Castro" wearing two Rolex watches worth $40,000. He was probably referring to former president Raul Castro, the brother of Fidel Castro, the leader of the Cuban revolution. The Assembly was discussing a resolution to be voted on Wednesday that would call for an end to the US embargo on Cuba, which has been tightening in recent months with a blockade on oil. Most of the nations that spoke opposed Washington's embargo and spoke in support of Cuba. Uganda's Permanent Representative Adonia Ayebare, speaking on behalf of the Nonaligned Movement, said the group "expresses its deep concern regarding the measures announced by the government of the United States this year, which tightened [the embargo]to unprecedented and extreme levels". Amid rumours of President Donald Trump planning an attack on Cuba, he said, "The Nonaligned Movement urges the General Assembly, as the most representative body of the United Nations, to mobilise efforts to prevent the military aggression against Cuba, a founding member of the Nonaligned Movement, and preserve peace". Singapore's Permanent Representative Burhan Gafoor, speaking on behalf of the ASEAN, said the organisation "is particularly concerned about the impact of the embargo on the Cuban people, especially their access to food, medicines and other essential supplies".

news.title: Trump factor looms as Herzog weighs next move in election deadlock
news.text: President Isaac Herzog has a particularly important role to play now that the election is over. He must decide who will receive the first mandate to form a government: Benjamin Netanyahu, Gadi Eisenkot or perhaps another candidate. Sources close to Herzog say he currently prefers to wait for the official election results, which are expected in several days, before addressing the issue and inviting party representatives to the President's Residence for consultations. Central Elections Committee Chairman Supreme Court Deputy Chief Justice Noam Sohlberg told Herzog on Tuesday that he expects to submit the official results only next Wednesday, although the results themselves are expected to be published several days earlier. The immediate implication is that Israel is entering a period of uncertainty against the backdrop of a sensitive security situation and the approaching U.S. midterm elections. Until then, according to prevailing assessments, no unusual security developments are expected. The central question is whether the political picture will become clearer and whether the White House and U.S. President Donald Trump will seek to intervene. Sources close to Trump are holding talks overnight with Israeli officials to understand the exit poll results, the prospects of forming a unity government and the significance of the largest party in determining who will form the next government. Washington does not want to see another government that includes far-right elements such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and would prefer a unity government or a stable coalition. The anti-Netanyahu bloc is concerned that the premier could attempt to trigger a regional escalation to complicate its efforts, and perhaps even force an emergency government with Yashar! Chairman Gadi Eisenkot. Eisenkot has categorically ruled out such a possibility, declaring that if it happened, he would "resign the next day." According to most of Tuesday evening's exit polls, neither bloc has secured the 61 Knesset seats needed to form a government, partly due to the strong showing by the Arab parties. Based on the average of exit polls published by Channels 11, 12 and 13, the predominantly Arab Joint List and Ra'am parties are projected to win a combined 18 seats. As a result, Israel appears headed for a politically complicated period alongside an already complex diplomatic and security situation. All three main television networks project a narrow advantage for the anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Eisenkot, with 52 seats compared with 50 for Netanyahu's bloc. In the days leading up to the election, Trump published two messages endorsing Netanyahu, the latest just over 24 hours before polling stations opened across Israel at 7 a.m. Tuesday. The anti-Netanyahu bloc is concerned that, in the absence of a decisive outcome between the two camps, as the exit polls currently suggest, Trump may seek to assist Netanyahu once more. Sources close to Trump's White House have offered several explanations in recent days for the president's support for Netanyahu. One was the claim that "Netanyahu promised Trump a unity government." Opposition figures, however, believe the endorsement post was effectively compensation for Netanyahu over the postponement of a possible strike on Iran until after the U.S. midterm elections, if such an operation ultimately takes place.
news.summary: As president awaits official election results, opposition leaders fear renewed Trump intervention after his two endorsements of Netanyahu, with political uncertainty mounting amid security tensions and approaching US midterms
news.author: Itamar Eichner

news.title: Pakistan warns against escalation in Iran crisis, urges diplomacy
news.text:
WASHINGTON: Pakistan has warned that the situation surrounding Iran’s nuclear programme has sharply deteriorated, urging all sides to exercise restraint and resolve the dispute through diplomacy amid continued hostilities and divisions within the UN Security Council.

Speaking at a council briefing on Iran and nuclear non-proliferation on Tuesday, Pakistan’s Acting Permanent Representative, Ambassador Usman Jadoon, said mounting tensions and a lack of consensus had made a diplomatic settlement more urgent.

“Pakistan remains concerned that the situation regarding the Iran nuclear file has sharply deteriorated, negatively impacting the consideration of the issue, including in the Security Council,” he said.

The dispute centres on international concerns over Iran’s nuclear activities and the verification of its commitments under the non-proliferation regime. The 2015 nuclear agreement between Iran and world powers sought to limit Tehran’s nuclear programme in exchange for sanctions relief, but the United States withdrew from the accord in 2018 during Donald Trump’s first presidency. Subsequent efforts to restore the agreement failed.

Mr Jadoon urged all parties to avoid rhetoric and actions that could aggravate the situation.

“Pakistan urges all sides to exercise restraint, refrain from irresponsible and destabilizing rhetoric, actions, and postures that could escalate tensions and increase the risk of conflict, and choose a path that delivers peace, security and stability for all,” he said.

Pakistan also called for the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to be allowed to address technical questions relating to the nuclear dispute without political interference.

“We have consistently maintained that any issues of non-compliance must be addressed through competent technical bodies like the IAEA, without politicization and consistent with the relevant parties’ rights and obligations,” Mr Jadoon said.

“The IAEA must be enabled to carry out its work without any hindrance and within its technical mandate,” he added.

The Pakistani envoy highlighted Islamabad’s diplomatic efforts to promote de-escalation, a ceasefire and negotiations. He cited the memorandum of understanding signed in Islamabad in June as evidence that diplomatic engagement could make progress.

“The Islamabad MoU signed in June is a successful manifestation of this approach. It demonstrates that progress on the diplomatic track is possible,” he said.

He acknowledged the support of Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, Egypt, China and other partners, and said Pakistan’s leadership continued working towards a peaceful settlement.

“We believe that diplomacy can once again deliver results in paving the way for settling contentious issues peacefully,” Mr Jadoon said.

Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot and his wife Hannah leave the polling station after voting in Herzliya on October 27, 2026, on the day of Israel's legislative election. A deeply divided Israel headed to the polls for the first time since Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack, with voters delivering their verdict on veteran prime minister and the country's rightward drift. (Photo by Jack GUEZ / AFP) 

 International News, Latest News 

October 27, 2026




 Israel opposition holds narrow edge over Netanyahu in first projections 







JERUSALEM, Undefined (AFP)—Israeli voters on Tuesday gave a narrow edge to opposition parties over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, initial projections showed, after decades-high turnout in the country’s first election since the trauma of the October 7, 2023 attacks.

Netanyahu, Israel’s longest serving prime minister, had run on promises to fight enemies from Hamas to Iran and had spent election day raising fears of Israeli Arab voters who came out in historic numbers against his hard-right government.

Early projections broadcast by Israeli television networks showed that no party would take an absolute majority but that the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, a centre-right former military chief, enjoyed a small advantage.

“The initial exit poll results indicate a complete lack of confidence in Netanyahu and the October 7 government,” Eisenkot said after polling stations closed.

Yair Lapid, a centrist former prime minister allied with Eisenkot, described the result as a “crushing defeat” for Netanyahu.

At Eisenkot’s watch party in a Tel Aviv sports arena, cheering supporters described the 66-year-old as the next prime minister and chanted, using Netanyahu’s nickname, “Bibi, go home!”

But Gideon Saar, Israel’s foreign minister and Netanyahu ally, said that victory declarations by the opposition were “premature”.

A new government may not take shape for weeks as Israeli politicians look to cobble together a government that can reach the magic number of 61 seats in the 120-member parliament.

The three mainstream networks — Channels 11, 12 and 13 — projected the opposition bloc to win 52 to 53 seats, and Netanyahu’s bloc to win 50, although his Likud would be the largest single party in the parliament, with 24 or 25 seats.

Israeli Arab lists were projected to win 17 to 18 seats, a sharp gain, potentially giving them a kingmaker role although Eisenkot has been coy on whether he would ally with them.

Political expert Tal Elovitz said that Netanyahu’s coalition had clearly lost ground and that Arab lawmakers gained.

“It appears there is a possibility of forming a minority government headed by Eisenkot, but this could still shift depending on the final results,” he said.

– Campaigning against Arab parties –

In a dash to secure as many votes as possible, Netanyahu had charged that Israeli Arabs were out to “steal the election” and his Likud party unsuccessfully asked election authorities to keep polls open past 10:00 pm.

His efforts led the opposition to charge that he was looking for pretexts to challenge the results.

Israelis cast their ballots in the shadow of October 7 and the multi-front regional wars that it sparked, with the trauma from the attack still fresh and questions over accountability and security central to the campaign.

The vote came as Israel looks increasingly isolated on the world stage, driven by the war in Iran and the military campaign in Gaza, soaring settlement construction and violence in the occupied West Bank.

Netanyahu himself faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court over Gaza as well as domestic corruption charges that could land him in prison.

Eisenkot, his main rival, is a political novice and former military chief whose mild manner is seen as the antithesis of the incumbent.

The son of working-class Moroccan Jewish immigrants, Eisenkot would be the first prime minister of Middle Eastern or North African descent.

Before voting, the 66-year-old Eisenkot paid his respects privately at the grave of his son Gal, whose death fighting in Gaza has drawn empathy from many Israelis.

Speaking afterwards at a polling station, Eisenkot called on Israelis to vote to replace “the worst government since the state was established”.

– Mass turnout –

Nationwide turnout as of 8:00 pm stood at nearly 75 percent, the highest in decades.

Some 7.3 million people were eligible to vote, with tens of thousands of Israelis estimated to have flown in from abroad for an election seen as crucial to deciding the future character of their country.

Eilana Zisblit, 55, told AFP she had travelled back from Canada, where she has lived for almost 30 years, to vote for a centre-right party in Eisenkot’s bloc.

“The country is going in a really, really bad direction. Both for Jews and Arabs living in the country, and for Jews living abroad,” she said.

The time to act is “now, or the country really won’t survive anymore”.

Netanyahu, 77, who has served as prime minister on and off for more than 19 years, has been quick to allege electoral fraud.

He said Tuesday that three senior officials of the United Arab List had been arrested with envelopes full of cash in the south.

The acting director general of the Central Elections Committee, Dean Livne, said that police had “caught individuals who tried to bribe voters”, adding that the unidentified suspects were not at polling stations and were caught near their homes.

He said the matter was a localised case and under investigation.

United Arab List head Mansour Abbas, who could emerge as a kingmaker in a close election, accused Netanyahu of “lying and inciting” to mobilise his voters.

Netanyahu last returned to power in December 2022, bringing into his coalition far-right ultra-nationalists who have aggressively championed settlements in the West Bank.

In the last days of the campaign, he posted an image of a nuclear bomb destroying Tel Aviv and talked up his endorsement by US President Donald Trump, who is also fond of alleging election fraud.

news.title: US agency is again probing if Polymarket broke 2022 settlement, sources says
news.text: A US regulator is investigating whether prediction market operator Polymarket violated a 2022 enforcement deal in which it promised to ban US users from its main overseas platform, reviving an inquiry the agency shuttered last year without bringing charges, said two people familiar with the matter.The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is probing whether Polymarket took sufficient steps to keep US users off the platform as part of a broader investigation it opened into the company earlier this year, the people said. One of the people said the scrutiny is focused on Polymarket's past controls and processes.The agency is examining Polymarket's controls for determining where customers are located, as well as its advertising activities in the United States, as part of that inquiry, the people said.Polymarket is based in New York and has an offshore entity registered in Panama.The CFTC is also scrutinizing Polymarket's US platform, which the company began rolling out late last year, including its customer onboarding processes and customer protections, said the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential enforcement issues.Reuters is reporting these elements of the probe for the first time. The Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg News and other media first reported in June that the CFTC was broadly probing Polymarket, but provided few details. Bloomberg added that the CFTC was looking into social media activity tied to the company.Spokespeople for the CFTC and Polymarket declined to comment. Probes are not necessarily an indication of wrongdoing and many do not result in enforcement action.The new details, nevertheless, raise fresh questions over why the CFTC and Justice Department last year closed similar probes into whether Polymarket had violated the 2022 settlement, which resolved CFTC allegations at the time that Polymarket had been operating in the US unlawfully since its launch in 2020.Neither agency has commented on the decision to close the probes and a Justice Department spokesperson declined to comment for this story.Prediction markets allow traders to bet on real-world events, including sports, government policy announcements and elections. Aided by supportive policies under President Donald Trump's second administration, the industry has surged over the past two years. Trump's son, Donald Trump Jr, is a Polymarket investor.As the platforms have grown, they have drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers and advocacy groups worried the platforms are creating new avenues for insider trading, while recent political upsets, including in Brazil this week, have raised questions about their accuracy.Polymarket has said it has revamped controls. The firm says it expressly prohibits the use of virtual private networks (VPNs) or similar tools to circumvent its geographic restrictions, and has extensive controls to monitor for misconduct and to prevent restricted users from accessing its offshore platform.Speaking to Reuters in August, Shana Bautista, Polymarket's global head of investigations and intelligence, said US users circumventing its restrictions was not "a really prevalent issue."BIDEN ADMINISTRATION AGENCIES OPENED PROBE IN 2024Under the 2022 settlement negotiated by the CFTC's former Biden-era leadership, Polymarket agreed to stop offering its market to US users. But as 2024 US election bets on the platform grew, political pundits and social media users questioned whether Americans were circumventing Polymarket's restrictions.Months before the election, the CFTC opened a probe into whether Polymarket was complying with the deal, Reuters and other media reported at the time. The Justice Department opened a related investigation, with the FBI searching Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan's New York home in November 2024.Two months later, the Trump administration took office and appointed new leaders to both agencies. On July 15, 2025, Coplan said in an X post that the CFTC and Justice Department had closed their probes and cleared the company of any wrongdoing.A week later, Polymarket said it had bought a CFTC-licensed derivatives exchange, which became the platform for its US operation. CFTC-registered platforms must comply with certain customer protection and market abuse prevention requirements.While CFTC data shows the agency's overall enforcement activity has slumped during Trump's second presidency, its enforcement director David Miller said during his first month on the job in March that he would aggressively police prediction markets.In April, the agency and Justice Department charged a US soldier, alleging he made $400,000 from insider bets on Polymarket's offshore platform, sparking fresh questions about its controls.According to the indictment, Gannon Ken Van Dyke, who has pleaded not guilty, accessed the platform using a VPN and "exit mode," which geolocated to a foreign country. Polymarket said at the time that it had referred the matter to the authorities.

news.title: World News | Hackers Target US Election Watchdog's Filing System Days Before Midterm Polls: Report
news.text:
New York [US], October 28 (ANI): The US Federal Election Commission (FEC) was targeted by a hacker or hackers, disrupting its electronic filing system days before the November 3 midterm elections, Reuters reported in an exclusive report, citing an email seen by the news agency.

The outage comes as political groups and super PACs spend record amounts in the final days of the election campaign, which will determine whether US President Donald Trump's Republican Party retains its majorities in Congress.

Also Read | 'Higher-Than-Usual Turnout in Left Strongholds': Benjamin Netanyahu Urges His Supporters As Israel Records High Early Poll Turnout.

In a statement, the FEC said its electronic filing system was offline, adding that its information technology staff were working to restore the service. An email sent by an FEC electronic filings officer to campaign compliance firms on Monday night (local time) said, "We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems. As a result, we've had to temporarily shut down our web-facing services," according to Reuters.

The outage has prevented political organisations from filing mandatory 24-hour and 48-hour campaign spending reports, which provide information about spending on specific races. However, users could still search the FEC website for previously filed reports, Reuters reported.

Also Read | China Tech Stocks Plunge Amid AI Slump, Wiping Out USD 480 Billion in Market Value.

The FEC later said the issue had been identified and a fix was being implemented. The agency did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment, while the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the Federal Bureau of Investigation referred questions to the FEC.

The FEC tracks campaign spending by candidates and political committees but does not administer US elections. The disruption is therefore not expected to affect voters' ability to cast their ballots.

The cyber incident comes as Trump has emphasised election integrity ahead of the November 3 polls, which will determine control of both chambers of Congress and influence his legislative agenda for the remainder of his term.

Trump has said he would respect the midterm election results if the polls were conducted honestly, while warning that he could use his veto power if necessary.

"We'll figure a way. I have a strong veto. I hope that won't be the case, but if it is, that's happened before… I will -- if they're honest elections," Trump told reporters.

Earlier, Trump announced a USD 1 million reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of individuals involved in voter fraud linked to previous elections or the upcoming 2026 midterms.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said, "Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid $1,000,000 upon the arrest and conviction of those who created the Fraud! Thank you for your attention to this matter."

The November 3 elections will see all 435 seats in the House of Representatives contested, along with approximately one-third of the Senate seats. The results are expected to shape the balance of political power in Washington and determine the extent to which the administration can advance its policy priorities.

According to a CBS News poll published on Sunday, Democrats are projected to win 229 seats in the House, potentially securing a majority, although Republicans retain a narrow path to holding control.

The CBS News/YouGov survey, conducted among 2,355 US adults between October 21 and 23, found that inflation, rising prices and broader economic concerns remain central to voters' decisions. It also indicated that many voters are motivated by opposition to the rival party rather than confidence in their preferred party's policy agenda.

The survey further found that more Democratic voters said they were certain to vote or had already voted early, while less committed voters tended to lean Republican, making turnout a potentially decisive factor. (ANI)

ANI brings the latest news on Politics and Current Affairs in India & around the World, Sports, Health, Fitness, Entertainment, & News. news.title: US costs of Iran war rise to over $47 billion, according to Pentagon estimate
news.text:
WASHINGTON: The US military has spent over $47 billion so far to prosecute the war in Iran, more than 25% higher than the Defense Department’s estimate in July, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters.

The Pentagon did not immediately ​respond to a request for comment on its estimate, which has not been shared publicly.

The disclosure ​about the rising cost of the Iran war comes as Republicans wrestle with the ⁠political fallout of the unpopular conflict ahead of the November 3 election that will determine control of ​Congress for the next two years.

The war’s impact on global energy costs has weighed on support for Republican candidates ​and hurt President Donald Trump’s approval ratings.

Trump’s Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.

The Pentagon’s latest estimate was tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29 billion ​to replace expended munitions used in the conflict.

More than $6 billion would be needed to replace military equipment ​and so-called “platform losses,” which include the loss of aircraft including many drones lost during the war.

Trump launched the Iran war ‌jointly with ⁠Israel in February, predicting that the conflict would last a short time.

Trump’s initial strategy in the Iran war focused on first using expensive, high-end precision missiles to bomb Iran’s defenses so it could later use less expensive munitions, including gravity bombs like the air-launched JDAMs, which are plentiful.

But an April ceasefire gave time for Iran ​to dig out underground storage ​facilities, bringing back online ⁠some Iranian defenses, as well as missiles and drones that had been inaccessible.

Trump has since imposed a naval blockade on Iran to starve it of oil export ​revenue and held out the possibility of restarting combat operations after the midterm elections. ​

US officials, ⁠speaking on condition of anonymity, say the Pentagon has been planning to restart heavy fighting if ordered to do so.

The latest Pentagon estimate compares to Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s July estimate of $37.5 billion for the cost of the war.

While ⁠the figures ​include a host of operational costs, from flight operations to ​cyber support, the US military’s Iran war cost estimates did not clearly account for the massive expense expected to repair damage to US ​bases sustained by Iranian missile and drone attacks.

news.title: The timeline of Flávio Bolsonaro's escape from Brazil after failed election
news.text:
Failed presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro has fled Brazil for the United States, which has confirmed it will grant him and his family entry visas.

It comes a day after Mr Bolsonaro vowed to remain in the South American nation to lead the political opposition against Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula.

But over a three-day period, the far-right senator's exact whereabouts and exit path out of Brazil have become shrouded in mystery.

Here is what we know about the timeline of his escape.

Saturday, October 24, local time: The idea of Senator Bolsonaro fleeing Brazil if he lost the presidential election was first raised by his brother, Eduardo, on a podcast. Eduardo suggested his brother was fearful of political persecution in Brazil amid ongoing corruption and money laundering investigations.

7pm, local Brazilian time, Sunday, October 25 (8am Monday AEST): Polls closed across Brazil after a two-hour voting extension was granted by Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin, following a request from President Lula's campaign.

10pm, Sunday, October 25: The Tribunal Superior Electoral, Brazil's electoral authority, announced Lula as the winner of the presidential election with 51.79 per cent of the vote, securing him a fourth term in office.

10:40pm, Sunday, October 25: Senator Bolsonaro delivered a three-minute address to the media near his electoral bunker in the Brazilian capital Brasília, saying he would not concede to Lula and would ask for the election result to be annulled. 

3:45pm, local Washington DC time, Monday, October 26 (5:45am Tuesday AEST): US President Donald Trump told reporters he believed the Brazilian election had been "rigged" and said he believed the way it had been administered "looked very bad". 

5pm, local Brazilian time, Monday, October 26 (6am Tuesday AEST): Senator Bolsonaro posted an Instagram video claiming he was handed a court order for him to surrender his passports. He then promised to hand his documents over and stay in Brazil to spearhead the political opposition to Lula.

11am, Tuesday, October 27: Senator Bolsonaro missed the court deadline to turn in his passports — which were then cancelled — to federal police, according to police sources who spoke with Reuters. Local media and the AFP news agency reported the senator had not been seen at his residence in Brasilia throughout the morning.At about the same time, local media reports began to surface that the senator had fled Brazil on a plane destined for the US. 

1:45pm, Tuesday, October 27: The leadership of President Lula's Workers' Party in Brazil's lower house confirmed a preventative detention order has been filed and a request made for an INTERPOL red notice arrest alert to be issued worldwide for Senator Bolsonaro. 

2:15pm, Tuesday, October 27: While Argentine officials denied Senator Bolsonaro entered the country from Brazil, local media reported a pilot confirmed a private jet was flown from Buenos Aires to the border town of Puerto Iguazú. 

The pilot said he believed the jet was to pick up four passengers, including the senator. No confirmation was made that the aircraft then departed Argentina.

2:30pm, Tuesday, October 27: Mauricio Marcon, the deputy leader of Senator Bolsonaro's Liberal Party, also said he believed Senator Bolsonaro had fled "into exile" in the US. 

6:15pm, Tuesday, October 27: Re-elected President Lula described Senator Bolsonaro's departure as "shameful" during his 81st birthday celebration in Brasilia. He said the senator treated Brazil as his "second country", behind "licking American boots"."Those who are not liable do not fear. A fellow that secretly leaves his country, that's because he is liable for something," he said.

6:30pm, Tuesday, October 27: A senior official with the US State Department confirmed to the ABC that it would "issue visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States". 

10pm, Tuesday, October 27: Media outlets including CNN, The Washington Post and the BBC independently reported Senator Bolsonaro had landed in the US, quoting unnamed sources. The BBC reported he arrived in Florida, where he met his brother Eduardo.

There remains no official confirmation of Senator Bolsonaro's arrival in the US, his location or the path he took to flee Brazil.

Local authorities continue to say there is no record of him crossing the border from Brazil into Argentina, and The Washington Post has also reported an anonymous Brazilian foreign ministry claim he may have passed through Venezuela.
news.summary: Failed presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro has fled Brazil for the United States, which has confirmed it will grant him and his family entry visas.

news.title: Vivek Ramaswamy edges Acton 47-45 in industry-sponsored Ohio poll as Trump rallies for him
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 28 (IANS) Indian American Republican Vivek Ramaswamy holds a two-point edge over Democrat Amy Acton in Ohio’s governor’s race, according to a new poll commissioned by a tech industry group, as President Donald Trump heads to the state on Wednesday to campaign for him. The survey by Echelon Insights for NetChoice, a tech industry trade group, put Ramaswamy at 47 per cent and Acton at 45 per cent, with Libertarian Don Kissick at 4 per cent, WSYX/ABC6 reported. It was conducted October 16-23 among 508 likely voters and has a margin of error of 5.2 percentage points, meaning the race is a statistical dead heat. The same poll found 70 per cent support for State Issue 3, a proposed constitutional amendment requiring photo ID to vote, with 28 per cent opposed. Inflation and the cost of living topped voter concerns at 57 per cent, ahead of foreign policy at 24 per cent and healthcare costs at 21 per cent. WSYX noted that the survey “was commissioned by an industry trade association testing public sentiment on tech.” A separate poll sponsored by A Fight Worth Having, a super PAC, and conducted by its polling unit RedBox Research, showed Acton ahead 48.2 per cent to 43.8 per cent. That survey of 2,998 likely voters, taken October 20-23, has a margin of error of 4.6 points. It also showed Democrat Sherrod Brown leading Republican Senator Jon Husted 46.9 to 44.2 in the Senate race. Trump is set to hold a midterm rally at the Shoemaker Center on the Ohio University Chillicothe campus on Wednesday. It will be the president’s third campaign event in Ohio this month, for Husted and Ramaswamy, WLWT reported. Brown and Acton are holding a rally in Cincinnati at 5:30 pm the same day. Ramaswamy has been crisscrossing the state on a bus tour in the final week, with stops in Noble, Washington, Meigs, Licking and Knox counties. “The Second Amendment isn’t a recommendation, it’s a right,” he posted on X from a stop in Licking County. Both campaigns have also focused on data centres in the closing stretch, the Statehouse News Bureau reported. Ramaswamy, a biotech entrepreneur and the son of immigrants from Kerala, ran for the Republican presidential nomination in 2024 before endorsing Trump. If elected, he would be Ohio’s first Indian American governor. The election is on November 3.

news.title: ‘Let’s make it the 51st state’: Trump suggests US statehood for Venezuela at Texas oil rally
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 28 (IANS) US President Donald Trump has said Venezuela could “someday soon” become America’s 51st state with an elected governor instead of a president, as he showcased a tanker carrying Venezuelan crude at a campaign rally in Corpus Christi, Texas. “It will become a prosperous country, and who knows, maybe someday soon it will become a prosperous 51st state. That’s possible. Let’s make it. Let’s make it the 51st state. And instead of a president, we’ll have an election for a governor. How about that?” Trump told the rally at the Port of Corpus Christi on Tuesday. Pointing to a vessel docked nearby, he said: “See that little ship out there? It’s got one million barrels of oil on it from Venezuela. And we’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history.” “To the victor belong the spoils, right? But thanks to our big victory in our recent war with Venezuela,” he said, adding that the oil “is being provided to the United States at zero cost to the American taxpayer.” The remarks went further than his comments hours earlier at Joint Base Andrews, where he told reporters: “We took over Venezuela very successfully. And they’ve sent me as a gift, a boatload of a million barrels of oil.” At the rally, he moved from describing the cargo as a gift to openly floating annexation. Secretary of State Marco Rubio travelled with Trump and was invited on stage. “It’s an honor to work for the greatest country in the world, for the greatest president in the history of the United States of America,” Rubio said. Trump joked that he would “drop him off in Cuba” and said Rubio would “settle that one in about 15 minutes.” On the war with Iran, Trump said: “And you’ve got to understand that America did not start the war with Iran. Iran has been waging this war against America since 1979, killing many, many of our great people.” He acknowledged the impact on fuel prices. “I knew that oil would go up, I actually thought it would go up 2 or 3 times higher, and I was still willing to do it,” he said, adding: “It’s going to end very soon.” He also said “your country is making an absolute fortune because of the situation in the Middle East.” Trump was in Texas to campaign for Attorney General Ken Paxton, whom he called “the best attorney general in the history of Texas”, along with Governor Greg Abbott and other Republicans ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. news.title: Israeli exit polls suggest no clear winner with Eisenkot's bloc neck and neck with Netanyahu
news.text: TEL AVIV: As the first exit polls arrived in Israel's election, opposition supporters breathed a sigh of relief. But as a long night set in, nervousness grew on both sides in a tight race that is pivotal for the country.At exactly 10:00 pm, exit polls showed a narrow edge for the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff and political novice seeking to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader."I feel better," Kalanit Sharon, 37, told AFP as cheers erupted in the Tel Aviv hall packed with backers of Eisenkot and his Yashar party.But as the night wore on, exit polls shifted, with major television networks putting the two sides on equal footing -- with Arab lists, which could become kingmakers, making strong gains.The vote, the first general election since Hamas's unprecedented October 7, 2023 attack, drew 77.7 percent turnout, the highest since 1999.For Netanyahu, blamed by opponents for the security failures that led to the attack, and for refusing to establish an independent commission of inquiry, his political survival was at stake."Three years ago, the government abandoned us," said Ohad Ben Ami, a former hostage taken to the Gaza Strip by the Palestinian militant group Hamas."An Israeli citizen should never have spent a year and a half in Hamas tunnels when deals (with Hamas) were on the table" to secure the hostages' release, he said at Eisenkot's event.Another supporter of the former general, Noa Ayal, a 31-year-old soldier who said she had completed "more than 360 days of reserve duty", said she had been "waiting for this change for so long"."I have a lot of hope, and if Gadi doesn't become prime minister, it will undoubtedly be very difficult."Eisenkot -- who swapped his usual plain black shirt for a suit and tie -- promised to work swiftly to form a government. But it will be no small feat with neither side appearing to have secured the votes.Yaheli Lifshitz, a 23-year-old student, acknowledged the challenge."To form a new government, they'll have to break with established rules and norms and build alliances that have never existed before," he said..Netanyahu’s rival Eisenkot urges voters to unseat ‘worst govt’ in Israeli history.Netanyahu might be finished but his policies toward the Palestinians will largely endure.We have to wait At a Jerusalem convention centre rented by Netanyahu's Likud, a sense of uncertainty reigned.On a giant screen, a video montage celebrated the prime minister, showing hugs with US President Donald Trump alongside footage of military strikes from the assorted wars he has led since the Hamas attack.When the first exit polls came out, 70-year-old retiree Aliza Schukerman refused to concede defeat."We'll have to wait until tomorrow morning, when they've counted all the votes. It will take time," she said."I'm sure that by 10:00 am tomorrow we will know that we've won and that Bibi is prime minister again."Elie Pieprz, 53, struck a similarly confident note."Usually things move more in our favour as the night goes on and as the morning approaches," he said."I'm very optimistic. I feel the prime minister has performed better than some of the pre-campaign polls suggested."Asked what might happen if the opposition ultimately prevailed, Pieprz called for a coalition that would still include Likud, citing the conflict with Iran and the need to maintain strong ties with Washington."Trying to change course in the middle of the journey is not a good idea," he said.Anat Margolin, a 49-year-old engineer, was less confident."I don't know what to hope for because throughout the day you could feel the results were going to be unpredictable, that this wasn't what we'd prepared for," she said.A regular viewer of Channel 14, an outlet supportive of Netanyahu, Margolin said she had mostly heard predictions pointing to a victory for her candidate, not to an opposition lead, however narrow."We weren't hearing about that possibility," she said..A look at the main issues in Israeli elections seen as a referendum on Netanyahu.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Who Is Gadi Eisenkot? The Former Army Chief Challenging Netanyahu’s Grip On Israel
news.text:
Gadi Eisenkot, the man who could unseat Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, cuts an understated figure. Almost always dressed in black, he speaks halting English and often answers interview questions with bullet-point lists, reflecting the military culture that shaped him.
For some voters ahead of Tuesday’s general election, the 66-year-old’s lack of charisma could be one of his biggest strengths.
Serious and unassuming, Eisenkot stands in stark contrast to Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister. Netanyahu is known for his polished, American-accented English and his ability to deliver headline-grabbing soundbites on US television and social media.
From Military Chief To Netanyahu’s Main Challenger
Eisenkot served as Israel’s military chief of staff from 2015 to 2019. He has pledged to unite Israelis after Netanyahu’s divisive tenure, during which the country has shifted sharply to the right.
Polling has placed Eisenkot neck and neck with Netanyahu. He has promised to repair Israel’s international standing, which has suffered significant damage after three years of war in Gaza and violence in the occupied West Bank.
He has also vowed to crack down on extremist Israeli settlers in the West Bank who have attacked Palestinians with impunity. Condemning recent incidents in which settlers beat up an American journalist and a French mayor, Eisenkot described the violence as “Jewish terror” enabled by Netanyahu’s government.
However, Eisenkot is no dove on the Palestinian question. He has sought to position himself to the right of Netanyahu on some issues, pledging that there would be no Palestinian state. His campaign has also highlighted earlier footage of Netanyahu reluctantly expressing openness to Palestinian statehood under US pressure.
The Military Doctrine That Shaped His Reputation
Eisenkot’s military record remains central to his public image. During the 2006 war with Hezbollah, he devised the so-called “Dahiya doctrine”, named after a Beirut suburb. The strategy envisaged the use of overwhelming force against civilian infrastructure in areas populated by the Lebanese militant group.
Israel has since applied the doctrine in Gaza, where the resulting destruction has prompted accusations from critics that its actions amount to war crimes. Israel disputes those allegations.
His military background has helped define his political approach, even as he seeks to present himself as an alternative to Netanyahu’s leadership.
Eisenkot has also drawn public sympathy following the deaths of his son, Gal, and two nephews while fighting in Gaza. Their deaths have added a deeply personal dimension to his political campaign.
Appeal Beyond Netanyahu’s Base
Eisenkot’s background is another element of his appeal. The son of Moroccan Jewish immigrants, he grew up on Israel’s geographic periphery, unlike Netanyahu, who comes from an elite family and whose father was a prominent professor in the United States.
If elected, Eisenkot would become Israel’s first prime minister of Sephardic background, a term referring to Jews whose recent origins lie in the Middle East and North Africa.
His campaign has sought to reach voters across political divides by combining security-focused policies with promises of institutional reform.
On Gaza, Eisenkot has pledged to end Hamas rule within 18 months. He has said this could be achieved through the implementation of US President Donald Trump’s ceasefire plan, which envisages the gradual disarmament of Hamas and a transfer of power, or through what he called “creative operations” targeting the group’s military wing.
Military Service, Judicial Independence And Minority Rights
Eisenkot has also addressed growing resentment over exemptions from military service for religious students following three years of war. He has promised to limit these exemptions and introduce a “universal national service law” requiring ultra-Orthodox Jews and Arab citizens to undertake either military or civilian service.
Seeking to attract centrist and liberal voters, he has pledged to protect judicial independence, the rule of law, minority rights and a free press.
These commitments offer a contrast with Netanyahu’s polarising tenure and could help Eisenkot appeal to voters seeking political change without abandoning a security-focused approach.
At his final major rally before Tuesday’s election, Eisenkot made a direct appeal to Netanyahu supporters who were still undecided.
“Deep down, you too know that Israel cannot go on like this,” he said. “Israel needs change.”
His message captures the central question facing voters: whether Eisenkot’s low-key style, military credentials and promises of reform can persuade enough Israelis to bring Netanyahu’s long rule to an end.

news.title: U.S. to issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro as his whereabouts remain unclear
news.text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil — The United States says it will issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family, amid multiple reports that the defeated Brazilian presidential candidate has left the country following Sunday's election. His whereabouts have not been independently confirmed. 

Bolsonaro, a conservative politician and ally of President Donald Trump, lost Sunday's presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by more than four million votes, just three weeks after winning the first round. While Bolsonaro's Liberal Party has since recognized Lula's victory, Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat.

On Tuesday a senior U.S. administration official said that the State Department would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family, allowing them to enter the country.

The visa announcement comes as Bolsonaro faces multiple investigations in Brazil, including allegations of money laundering and tax evasion, which he denies. On Monday Brazil's Supreme Court ordered him to surrender his passports within 24 hours and barred him from leaving the country.

The order followed comments by Bolsonaro's brother Eduardo, who lives in self-imposed exile in Florida, suggesting Flávio should leave Brazil if he lost the election.

In a video released that day, Bolsonaro said federal police officers had stopped him outside the home of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, and ordered him to surrender his passports. The former far-right leader is under house arrest after being sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup following his own defeat by Lula in the 2022 presidential election.

"I never thought about leaving the country," Flávio Bolsonaro said in the video. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this aberration." He described the order as an attempt to intimidate him.

On Tuesday, Brazilian media reported that Bolsonaro had left for the United States. His campaign manager, his lawyer and other political allies had earlier said they did not know his whereabouts.

Lula won the election with just over 51% of the valid votes, or approximately 64.2 million, compared with more than 48%, or nearly 59.8 million, for Bolsonaro.

President Trump has repeatedly cast doubt on Lula's victory, suggesting on Monday that the election was "rigged", without offering any evidence. He returned to the subject at a campaign rally in Texas on Tuesday night, as he accused Democrats of election fraud.

"Brazil is also doing a good job of it, aren't they? Did you see that? I didn't take sides, but it didn't look very good," he said.

Lula criticised Bolsonaro's reported departure during celebrations for his 81st birthday in Brasília on Tuesday.

"Those who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear," Lula told supporters.

"He could have stayed and proven that the accusations [against him] are not true," Lula said, adding that he regretted Bolsonaro's departure.

He also took aim at the Bolsonaro family's close ties to the Trump administration. "Brazil is their second home; their first home is the United States," he said.
news.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro leaves Brazil for the U.S. amid a money-laundering probe, as Washington agrees to issue visas to him and his family.

news.title: Trump Humiliates Must-Win MAGA Candidate After Man-Thirst Rant
news.text:
President Donald Trump has declared that his MAGA pick for the Texas Senate is just not hot enough.

The looks-obsessed Trump, 80, slighted Ken Paxton’s appearance during a rally for the scandal-ridden candidate in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday night.

He insulted the state attorney general immediately after praising fellow GOP Senate hopeful, incumbent Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, who has been the apple of Trump’s eye for most of October.

“So I’m studying him, and I made the mistake of saying that I started off by studying his a--,” Trump said, describing his fascination with Husted’s posterior. “And then I looked at his feet, and they were massive.”

The president continued on, fawning over the former college football player’s hands, his “fingers like sausages,” and his shoulders.

“But I made the mistake of studying his anatomy and explaining it to the audience, and the audience loved it,” Trump rambled. “By the way, he went up 12 points that day. He went from being down to being up.”

Most polls show him and Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown in a tight race, with Brown even maintaining a slight edge over the incumbent senator.

The president and former teen beauty pageant judge then turned his attention to Paxton, though his next statement was much less flattering.

“Maybe I should do that with Ken Paxton, but I’m not sure your body is gonna qualify,” Trump said. “I’m gonna do it with Ken!”

The Daily Beast has reached out to the White House and both Husted and Paxton’s campaigns for comment.

The president has made his weird fascination with Husted’s body a staple of his panic tour across America.

The incumbent Ohio senator addressed Trump’s repeated mentions of his body earlier on Tuesday, telling reporters, “Don’t worry, I was in the weight room this morning working out. I don’t want to let him down.”

While Trump has been keen to compliment Husted’s a--, he considers Paxton to be more of a pain in one.

“He’s been a friend of mine for a long time, one of the most loyal people. When I was being hit by the radical left very hard, harder than very few people could have withstood it, Ken Paxton was at my side more than anybody,” he said of Paxton at a rally in Denton, Texas, early this month. “I have to always remember that, because he could be a pain in the a-- sometimes. I’ll be honest.”

The president has also roasted Paxton’s looks, going so far as to call him ugly during a dinner at the Rose Garden in early September.

“Ken Paxton, you might not like the way he dresses. And I say this, it’s so insulting to him, but I might as well say it,” Trump said on Sept. 2. “You might not... like the way he looks. You might not love his look. You might not love his television interviews.”

About a week later, he shared more critiques of Paxton’s appearance on the last night of the Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas.

“I have to say this about Ken. It’s so insulting, and I hope he doesn’t get insulted,” he said at his so-called “Trump-a-Palooza. ”He may not dress right. He may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen, but you know what he is? He’s the greatest attorney general in America, and he deserves to be your next senator."

The looks-obsessed Trump, 80, slighted Ken Paxton’s appearance during a rally for the scandal-ridden candidate in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday night.
