news.title: Supervisors call for answers about death at  Otay Mesa Detention Center
news.text:
San Diego officials expressed concern Tuesday after an immigrant detainee’s death at Otay Mesa Detention Center, continuing what civil rights activists and other critics call a grim trend of increasing deaths in ICE custody.

Shortly after 11:30 a.m. Saturday, a staff member at the Department of Homeland Security facility “called a medical emergency after finding an unresponsive (detained) individual in their assigned living area,” according to a statement from CoreCivic, the private-prison company that runs the center.

“Responding medical staff arrived quickly, began lifesaving measures and called for emergency medical services … EMS arrived and continued those efforts, but the individual was pronounced deceased before being transported from the facility,” the statement said.

The company released no further information about the person or the circumstances of the death.

“We are deeply saddened by the loss of anyone in our care,” the Tennessee-based company stated. “Our government partners at U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement … were notified immediately.”

ICE did not respond to a request for comment.

During a news conference Tuesday, county Supervisors Paloma Aguirre and Terra Lawson-Remer called on the Trump administration and CoreCivic to cooperate with county investigators and clear the way for ongoing inspections at the Otay Mesa center, near the U.S.-Mexico border.

“Earlier this year, we took ICE to federal court for blocking public health inspections amid disturbing reports of unsafe conditions at Otay Mesa,” Lawson-Remer said. “Now a man has died inside that facility. When the federal government flouts due process and shuts the door on independent health inspectors, we cannot look away. We need answers, accountability and the ability to protect the health and safety of everyone held inside.”

The lawsuit “wasn’t a political exercise – it was a necessary step to protect human lives,” Aguirre said.

“Ensuring basic human rights, medical oversight and safety within our borders is non-negotiable,” she said. “ICE and CoreCivic must be held accountable for these failures right now, before another family is forced to suffer this same unimaginable grief.”

The San Diego County Medical Examiner’s Office conducted an autopsy on the detainee Monday, according to the supervisors. A cause of death has yet to be released.

During their briefing, Aguirre and Lawson-Remer also announced that they had sent a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and acting ICE Director David Venturella demanding that the latter agency and CoreCivic take the following steps:

Cooperate fully with the medical examiner’s investigation, including making staff available for interviews and turning over all requested records, logs and video;

Preserve all data related to the death, including medical records, any sick-call requests, housing-unit logs staff rounds and video;

Provide a timeline of care from intake to death, including any health conditions noted upon the person’s entry, requests for medical help, medical visits and welfare checks;

Where privacy law requires it, share this information with the family and, with their consent, with the county;

Provide a written accounting of corrective actions taken since the county inspection in June, including improvements to tuberculosis reporting, vaccine supply and any delays in providing prescribed medical devices;

Confirm that the appropriate consulate has been notified if the decedent was a foreign national and publish ICE’s death notice and detainee death report without delay; and

Allow ongoing inspection access under county public health authority so its team can verify that the listed measures are being taken.

After ICE denied supervisors access to the detention center, the county sued and secured a federal court order allowing an inspection in June.

That scrutiny identified failures to promptly report suspected tuberculosis cases, a lack of vaccines in stock and delays in providing necessary medical equipment, according to the supervisors. 

In September, the county issued another notice of noncompliance after a suspected tuberculosis case allegedly went unreported for about three weeks.

The county’s public health officer is evaluating additional oversight measures, including follow-up inspections. Litigation over the county’s ongoing inspection authority remains unresolved, with the parties slated to meet again this Thursday.

Aguirre and Lawson-Remer requested a written response from federal officials by Nov. 10.

While exact numbers of such fatalities are elusive, the ACLU claimed last month that at least 57 people have died while in U.S. immigration detention since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term – more than double the number of deaths recorded in the previous four years combined.

According to a Human Rights Watch report released in June, the mortality rate of ICE detainees – based on 52 known deaths at the time – had reached its highest level in over a decade and more than doubled since Trump’s current term began. The rate at that time was nearly four times that of the Biden administration, and more than 2 1/2 times as high as that of the first Trump administration, the watchdog organization reported.

“Urgent action is needed to address this crisis and prevent further deaths,” the report concluded.
news.summary: The county Medical Examiner's Office conducted an autopsy on the detainee Monday, according to the supervisors. A cause of death has yet to be released.

news.title: Grand Jury Declines to Indict Cassidy Hutchinson for Her Jan. 6 Testimony
news.text:
A grand jury has declined to indict former White House staffer Cassidy Hutchinson for her testimony about President Donald Trump’s alleged conduct during the January 6 riot on Capitol Hill in 2021.

The Justice Department sought to prosecute Hutchinson for reasons that have not yet been made clear due to the confidentiality of the case, but President Trump and Republicans had previously accused her of lying under oath during her testimony about January 6 before the House committee. Sources close to the case confirmed to the Associated Press (AP) that the grand jury declined to prosecute while providing few details:

A grand jury in Washington rejected prosecutors’ request to return an indictment against Cassidy Hutchinson, said the people, who spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the case.
Details of prosecutors’ allegations against Hutchinson were not immediately clear, but Republican lawmakers had accused her of lying under oath in her explosive testimony in 2022 about Trump’s behavior on Jan. 6.
She described an angry, defiant president who was trying to let armed protesters avoid security screenings at a rally that morning to protest his 2020 election defeat and who later grabbed at the steering wheel of the presidential SUV when the Secret Service refused to let him go to the Capitol. And when the events at the Capitol spiraled toward violence, with the crowd chanting “Hang Mike Pence,” she testified that Trump declined to intervene.

Hutchinson did, however, admit during her testimony that she was only relaying information she had obtained from a White House security official, emphasizing that she was not a personal eyewitness.

Trump had called Hutchinson a “total phony” and “bad news,” denying her allegations.

In 2024, House Republicans also released a transcript of the January 6 Committee’s interview with the Secret Service officer who drove the presidential SUV, which contradicted some of Hutchinson’s claims. While the driver did say that President Trump was insistent about going to the Capitol during the riot, he rejected the claim that the president tried to grab the steering wheel.

“I didn’t see him, you know, lunge to try to get into the front seat at all,” the driver said.

According to Fox News, the federal grand jury “had heard evidence concerning possible false statements Hutchinson made to the congressional committee.”

“The grand jury’s decision not to indict Hutchinson does not establish whether her congressional testimony was truthful or false. Hutchinson has previously maintained that she stands by her testimony,” it added.
news.summary:
A grand jury has declined to indict former White House staffer Cassidy Hutchinson for her testimony about President Donald Trump's alleged conduct during the January 6 riot on Capitol Hill in 2021.

news.title: H-1B $100,000 fee case: Plaintiffs push for summary judgment, Trump administration seeks pause
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 28 (IANS) Employers and workers challenging the Trump administration’s $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions have asked a federal court in California to move quickly towards a final ruling, while the government wants the case put on hold until an appeals court rules. In their joint case management statement in Global Nurse Force v. Trump, filed on October 20, the plaintiffs said they “challenge the lawfulness of a $100,000 payment requirement as a condition of processing H-1B visa petitions and entry into the United States.” On September 30, Judge Gilliam granted in part the plaintiffs’ motion for a preliminary injunction, denied the government’s motion to dismiss and denied class certification without prejudice. The government appealed to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals on October 9 and the same day moved to stay the district court proceedings. That stay motion is set for a hearing on January 14, 2027, according to the filing. The plaintiffs proposed that the government produce the administrative record by November 3. “Plaintiffs are monitoring Defendants’ compliance with this Court’s September 30, 2026 order and may seek enforcement of the order if warranted,” the statement said. The government argued that going ahead now would be wasteful. “Defendants maintain that further motions practice is inappropriate while the Ninth Circuit considers threshold jurisdictional issues,” it said. It proposed that the record be produced only 30 days after the appeals court’s mandate, or 30 days after any order denying the stay. The government also pointed to a separate ruling in Massachusetts. “The outcome of this case will not change any status quo given the universal injunction entered in the District of Massachusetts,” it said, adding that further litigation “only wastes the Parties’ and Court’s resources, and might well result in a duplicative appeal.” The filing lists two other pending appeals on the fee: California v. Mullin in the First Circuit and Chamber of Commerce v. DHS in the District of Columbia Circuit, which was argued on March 9, 2026. The principal legal issues, the parties said, are whether the President’s proclamation and its extensions are “ultra vires”, and whether the actions of the State Department and the Department of Homeland Security to implement it violate the Administrative Procedure Act. President Donald Trump imposed the fee through Proclamation 10973, signed on September 19, 2025. He extended it with Proclamation 11069 on September 18, 2026. The plaintiffs are represented by groups including the Justice Action Center, Democracy Forward, the South Asian American Justice Collaborative (SAAJCO) and the law firm Cohen Milstein Sellers & Toll.

news.title: EU seeks to avoid Ukraine’s mistakes in relying on Starlink — Bloomberg
news.text:
NEW YORK, October 28. /TASS/. Discussions on strengthening defense capabilities have gained renewed momentum in the European Union following slowdowns in the operation of the Starlink satellite system in Ukraine, Bloomberg reported, citing sources.

According to the sources, one of the central topics at the latest EU summit on October 15-16 was the slowdown in Starlink services and the resulting new public dispute between Vladimir Zelensky and US President Donald Trump. European officials discussed the need to bolster their own capabilities, reduce dependence on the United States, and diversify suppliers of "critical technologies."

However, a Bloomberg source stressed that such changes would take years. The most realistic solution under the circumstances is to strengthen Europe’s role within existing structures, such as NATO, the agency added.

Last week, Kiev said that US company SpaceX had restricted the operation of Starlink terminals used by the Ukrainian armed forces, disrupting several Ukrainian military operations. SpaceX founder and entrepreneur Elon Musk, for his part, stated that the Starlink satellite system is not used for offensive military operations but only for defense and civilian purposes. He also said that Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government and that any restrictions are imposed by the US military and ultimately by the US president. Meanwhile, The Wall Street Journal claimed that Musk himself had ordered restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starshield.

On October 22, Trump announced that Ukraine’s access to the military-grade Starshield satellite communications system had been restored. However, he declined to answer a question about who had issued the order.

news.title: Begala: 'Trump Is the Problem, Not the Solution' for the Republican Party
news.text:
CNN analyst Paul Begala said Tuesday on “The Source” that President Donald Trump “is the problem, not the solution” for the Republican Party in the midterm elections.

Host Kaitlan Collins said, “James Tellico, the Democrat running for Senate in Texas, says this is an election, basically, he describes as a fight between David and Goliath. He’s running, of course, against Ken Paxton, the president’s chosen Republican candidate in that state. You’re our resident Texan here tonight. Do you think these two rallies today that the president held will be enough to get Ken Paxton over the finish line?”

Begala said, “I don’t. And I understand what the president is trying to do. He’s trying to rally the base. And I respect that. news.title: Trump Takes Obama Meltdown to Unhinged Level
news.text:
Donald Trump has taken his meltdown over former President Barack Obama to an unhinged new level.

Trump, 80, has made Obama a regular target of his ire in his rallies this month, particularly after the Democrat called out his gaudy taste over the weekend, comparing his tacky renovations at the White House to the Cheesecake Factory.

Speaking to media on Monday, Trump called Obama “a lousy president” and claimed “he’s not a smart guy,” while defending his beloved gold aesthetic and makeover skills.

During an afternoon rally on Tuesday in Corpus Christi, Texas, lifelong McDonald’s connoisseur Trump took a different turn and slammed Obama for his healthy diet.

The senior president began by shouting out his former White House physician Ronny Jackson, 59, who was at the rally in his current role as a Representative for Texas’s 13th congressional district, and is up for re-election.

Trump dusted off one of his go-to stories about Jackson being his White House physician as well as, Obama and George W. Bush. However, while Jackson served in the White House Medical Unit during George W. Bush’s administration, he was not actually Bush’s physician. Obama first named Jackson physician to the president in 2013.

Trump said, “They ask, ‘Doctor, who is the healthiest?’ ‘Cause he presided over the lives of Barack Hussein Obama and Bush and Trump, and they asked him... ‘Who’s the healthiest of the three?’ He said, ‘Without question, the healthiest is President Donald J. Trump.’ And I loved him.”

Trump continued his tirade against Obama by using a bizarre accusation over the former president’s eating habits.

“‘And a much better golfer,’” Trump added, still claiming to be quoting Jackson’s comments. “I am a much... that I will agree to. But no, no. But, you know, ‘cause Obama — every piece of lettuce he eats has to be perfect, and I don’t — I’m not that choosy.”

Trump’s unhealthy diet, which includes a steady intake of McDonalds, candy and Diet Coke, has even been called out by his own administration and his own family.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told podcaster Joe Rogan in January that Trump is “pumping himself full of poison all day long.”

The president’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, also revealed in his 2022 memoir Breaking History that Trump’s go-to order at McDonald’s is a Big Mac, Filet-O-Fish, fries, and a vanilla shake. 

The Big Mac does include shredded iceberg lettuce.

Trump has previously stated that Jackson said he was healthier than Obama, including at a campaign rally in Coralville, Iowa, in December 2023.

“I said, ‘Who’s healthier?’ He said, ‘Sir, there’s no contest.’ I won’t tell you the answer but you know the answer, OK? It was me.”

Newsweek found in 2024 that there was no public record of Jackson ever making that claim.

In January, 2018, Jackson claimed Trump has “incredibly good genes,” and said “I told the president if he had a healthier diet over the last 20 years he might live to be 200,” calling his overall health “excellent.”

Obama’s last BMI as president was 22.8 in 2016. Trump’s last physical, released in May, recorded his BMI as 29.7, which is at the very top of the overweight range and just below the obese category, which begins at 30.

The Daily Beast has contacted the White House and reps for Obama for comment.

news.title: Obama unloads on Trump while stumping for Democrats ahead of midterms
news.text:
US PRESIDENT Donald Trump has been telling voters to view the midterm elections as if he were on the ballot, and on Saturday one of his Democratic predecessors did just that.

Ten days out from the elections that will determine control of the closely divided Congress, Barack Obama took to the campaign trail to accuse the Republican president of corruption, deride his strategy for Iran and skewer the gilded aesthetic he has applied to White House renovations.

Mr. Obama stumped for Democratic candidates at rallies in Cleveland and Detroit, lampooning the Trump administration. Campaigning in Michigan for US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Mr. Obama framed the November 3 vote as a “circuit breaker” to “at least rein in some of the foolishness” of Mr. Trump’s presidency.

“We got to flip that circuit breaker, bring some accountability to this government,” Mr. Obama said.

Mr. Obama, president from 2009 until Mr. Trump began his first term in 2017, remains one of the most popular figures among Democrats. They hope that bringing him into the race can fire up their supporters for a tight US Senate race in which El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former US representative.

The former president obliged the Michigan crowd by playing to Democrats’ frequently repeated criticisms of Mr. Trump and of Republicans’ willingness to go along with him.

“We have never seen a president excel in straight-up grifting, on your dime, like this,” Mr. Obama said. “Never seen a president so intent on selling favors like this … Now the party seems to stand for corrupt government, or inept government, or no government.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll in August found that 63% of Americans think the president and his family have inappropriately profited from cryptocurrency since he returned to the White House last year and that 69% believe his policy decisions are influenced by his private business dealings.

Mr. Obama also ridiculed the administration’s claims of victory against Iran. He argued that the war has given Iran more economic leverage because its threats to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have unsettled oil exporters.

“Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil goes through to get to the world,” Mr. Obama said.

The former president also accused the Trump administration of emphasizing unimportant matters, sarcastically calling Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth someone “laser-focused on important matters like the jawline and testosterone levels of our troops” and ridiculing White House renovations as tacky.

news.title: Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro Flees to US After Election Loss
news.text: WASHINGTON: Defeated right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro left Brazil for the United States despite a court order banning him from exiting the country, US media reported Tuesday. The son of jailed ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro lost the presidential election Sunday to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and refused to concede defeat. The right-wing senator on Monday said a Supreme Court justice had ordered him to hand over his passports. Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering, and with his election loss is also set to lose parliamentary immunity. The 45-year-old arrived in the United States, CNN and the Washington Post reported, each citing an anonymous source. Where he landed remains unknown. The US State Department said Tuesday it would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family, without confirming his travel plans. A police source told AFP that the senator's Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been canceled, adding that "there is no formal record of Flavio Bolsonaro leaving the country." But he has held Italian nationality since 2023, according to an Italian parliamentary document seen by AFP. Bolsonaro's campaign manager Rogerio Marinho expressed shock over reports that the defeated candidate had fled Brazil. "We still don't have any news about his whereabouts," he told reporters Tuesday in Brasilia. "I received a text message from him this morning, where he said he would let some time pass today and then would talk with us, and that was it," Marinho said. "That was the only communication we had." - 'Shameful' - Lula called fleeing the country a "shameful" act. "A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide. The act of leaving Brazil is shameful," he remarked in Brasilia during his 81st birthday celebration. Bolsonaro said Monday that the ban on his exit from Brazil amounted to a scare tactic. "I never had any intention of leaving the country," he said in a video posted on Instagram. US President Donald Trump, a close ally of Jair Bolsonaro, on Monday said Brazil's elections were "rigged" following the defeat of Bolsonaro junior. Flavio's brother Eduardo, a US-based former lawmaker, maintains close ties with the White House. Last week, he told a US podcast that Flavio Bolsonaro should leave Brazil in the event of electoral defeat, given the active probes into his activities. In his Monday statement, Lula's challenger also said he would lead the opposition to the leftist government. Following Lula's victory with 51.8 percent of the vote, Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the result, citing the decision to extend polling hours over transportation difficulties that prevented some citizens from voting. Lula had requested the extension, as had Bolsonaro over bad weather in parts of the country. - In his father's footsteps - All bets were on a Bolsonaro win after he came out on top in the first round of elections earlier this month. He campaigned on a pledge to liberate his father, who is under house arrest for coup-plotting after his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro never conceded defeat and left the country on the eve of his rival's inauguration, only returning to Brazil three months later. Separately on Tuesday, the Supreme Court ordered police to investigate alleged foreign funding of Flavio Bolsonaro's campaign and other interference from abroad such as social media "manipulation." Lula's campaign complained about election interference by Meta, the parent company of WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, claiming "algorithmic manipulation." Meta denies taking any actions to favor one side in the election, but previously said that some of Lula's campaign ads had been mistakenly deactivated due to technical errors.

news.title: Netanyahu vows to confront Iran threat alongside Trump as exit polls show no clear majority
news.text: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu declared early Wednesday that his Likud party remained Israel's largest political force, according to election exit polls, and vowed to continue confronting Iran alongside U.S. President Donald Trump, even as projections showed his political bloc falling short of a parliamentary majority. Speaking after exit polls projected Likud as the largest party in the 120-member Knesset, Netanyahu said Israel had dramatically reshaped the Middle East through military operations against Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran, crediting the country's soldiers and his government's decisions for what he described as unprecedented strategic achievements. "We have accomplished wonders that have changed the face of the Middle East," Netanyahu said. "We eliminated Mohammed Deif, Yahya Sinwar, Hassan Nasrallah and Ali Khamenei. We established security zones in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria. We removed enormous threats hanging over us and struck the Iranian regime." "Iran is weaker than ever, and Israel is stronger than ever," he said, attributing those achievements to "our steadfast soldiers and the decisions we made." But Netanyahu stressed that Israel's military campaign was not finished, warning that Iran would continue to pose an existential threat as long as its current leadership remained in power. "This is not over as long as this fanatical regime exists," he said. "As long as it exists, it will try to destroy us. And together with our wonderful friend, President Trump, we will work to remove this threat once and for all." Netanyahu's remarks came as exit polls suggested his bloc had increased its parliamentary representation but remained below the 61 seats required to form a majority government, leaving Israel facing another potentially prolonged round of coalition negotiations.
news.summary: 'Israel is stronger than ever': Prime minister hails military achievements across the Middle East and says the fight against Iran is far from over, as exit polls project Likud as Israel's largest party but leave his political bloc short of a Knesset majority
news.author: Ilan Levinsohn

Samba the capybara is alive and well - and still on the run - more than six months after escaping from a Hampshire zoo. 
The runaway rodent and her sister Tango vanished from their enclosure at Marwell Zoo on March 17 while being moved to temporary accommodation. 
Tango was found soon afterwards, but Samba remained on the loose. 
Her great escape prompted a massive search operation and months later sightings have been few and far between.
But now the zoo has issued an update to say the mischievous fugitive has been spotted on newly-installed wildlife cameras on 'private land', with her keepers 'focused on bringing her home safely'.
In a statement issued on Tuesday, the zoo said: 'Since confirming that we had new photographic evidence of Samba’s whereabouts in August, our team has continued working tirelessly to bring her safely back to Marwell Zoo.
'Recovering Samba is a gradual and carefully managed process. Although we know the area she is in, it isn’t simply a case of being able to approach and collect her. 
'It’s vital that we keep any stress to an absolute minimum, as frightening or disturbing her could cause her to move away from the area and make her safe recovery more difficult.

Samba's disappearance has attracted widespread attention, with members of the public reporting possible sightings in recent months.

According to animal experts, a capybara could survive in the UK. The rodent has an abundant food source with plenty of grass and plants along riverbanks for it to eat.
They also have no natural predators that could hunt them. 
For Samba, the biggest risk to her life could come from traffic, while she might struggle to reach food sources due to freezing temperatures over the winter months. 
Capybaras are also social creatures often living in groups of 20 to 100 animals, and solitary capybaras can be prone to stress and depression.

news.title: Palestinian activist Khalil returns to Columbia after US detention
news.text:
NEW YORK: Mahmoud Khalil, a figurehead of Gaza war protests in the United States, returned Tuesday to Columbia University for the first time since his 2025 arrest under President Donald Trump’s crackdown on pro-Palestinian activists.

The 31-year-old told AFP his presence for an event on his new memoir, attended by around 100 people, was a “victory,” as he accused Columbia of seeking “to erase me, to erase any Palestinian voices on campus.”

He has slammed the Ivy League institution for its response to the 2024 student demonstrations, which included allowing New York police to clear protesters from its Manhattan campus in a heavy-handed operation.

Columbia said at the time the protests were a safety threat.

Khalil has also accused the university of failing to protect him from harassment ahead of his arrest by US immigration authorities and three-month detention without criminal charge, before his release in June 2025.

“Columbia could have been an example for how to have difficult conversations on campus, how to respond to such a protest, how to be aligned with human rights and with international law,” Khalil told AFP in an interview.

“They chose the total opposite. They chose brutality. They chose repression,” he said.

Some Jewish groups on social media had opposed Khalil’s return. A spokesperson for Columbia said the college is “committed to rigorous debate, inquiry, and respectful dialogue across differing perspectives.”

“Columbia supports the right of faculty members to organize academic events. An invitation to speak does not signify university endorsement of a speaker’s views,” they said in a statement carried by US media.

news.title: US will issue visa to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family after he fled Brazil following election loss... as he defies order to give up his passport
news.text:
The United States will issue Flávio Bolsonaro a visa after he fled Brazil following his devastating loss to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday's election, a senior State Department official said.

The official told the Daily Mail on Tuesday that the department will issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family 'and allow them entry into the United States.'

The announcement came just hours after Bolsonaro fled his native country, following the advice of his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in Texas and publicly encouraged Flávio to leave Brazil if he lost the election.

A spokesperson for Bolsonaro did not respond to a request for comment; his campaign manager Rogério Marinho also refused to comment.

But Bolsonaro has touted his relationship with President Donald Trump and even visited the White House in May. The family connections go deeper, with Eduardo Bolsonaro being convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration. He was sentenced to four years in prison and a warrant was recently issued for his arrest.

Trump did not offer a full-throated endorsement of Flavio Bolsonaro in the runoff against President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, as he has with some other right-of-center candidates in Latin America. But he suggested on Monday, without providing evidence, that Brazil's election was 'rigged.'

Bolsonaro's decision to leave Brazil came as a deadline for him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports expired at noon Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied.

Bolsonaro was served with the order to surrender his passports on Monday, just one day after his stunning loss. 

The far-right candidate said in a video posted to social media that he received the order outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula. Jair fled Brazil for Florida following the defeat, but returned three months later.

'I was ordered right on the street to hand ‌over ⁠my passports, and I'm also prohibited from leaving the country,' his son said in the video, as he denied that he was fleeing the country.

'I never thought about leaving the country,' Bolsonaro said in a video published on his social media channels. 'I will hand over my passports and I will defend myself from this aberration. It is a clear attempt to intimidate me. But I will not be silenced.' 

The sealed Supreme Court order for the younger Bolsonaro to hand over his passport, viewed by The Associated Press, was issued Sunday amid two federal investigations into the senator for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion.

In one, Bolsonaro is accused of using a sports betting company to launder more than $1 billion deductions from government pensions paid to senior citizens, according to The New York Times. 

In a separate case, Bolsonaro is accused of accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced banker at the center of a huge corruption scheme to finance a biopic of his father.

Prosecutors also suspect the funds from the banker were used to pay his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro's, expenses and to promote Flávio Bolsonaro's political agenda with the Trump administration, documents show. 

Bolsonaro has denied any wrongdoing in both cases, and has claimed Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who is heading one of the investigations, is a Lula ally. 

Mauricio Marcon, a lawmaker of Bolsonaro's Liberal Party, also questioned de Moraes' objectivity on Tuesday. 

'Seven minutes after the election, Alexandre de Moraes ordered his passports to be seized,' Marcon said. Bolsonaro 'will represent us in a free country. He will continue to be our leader.'

Meanwhile, Brazilians took to social media to ask where Bolsonaro was. Reporters gathered outside his home in the capital, Brasilia, but he did not appear. 

When Paulo Figueiredo, a close ally of Bolsonaro's who lives in the United States, was then asked about the senator's whereabouts, he did not answer directly.

'At this moment - following months of intense work that were unfairly thwarted - I have no desire to speak with the press. I kindly ask that you do not persist. Should I have a statement to make on any matter, I will reach out,' Figueiredo said.

Bolsonaro had refused to accept the election results for several hours following Sunday's election and even asked for the results to be annulled.

He ultimately accepted defeat in his video on Monday, but claimed Lula had used unfair tactics to win.

Bolsonaro then urged the electoral court to investigate alleged election fraud and nullify Lula's and Vice President Geraldo Alckmin's candidacies, which the electoral court has never done before.

To overturn the result, Bolsonaro would have to present evidence of fraud affecting Lula's 4.4 million-vote margin and convince the eight-member electoral court before the results are certified on December 18.

Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, received more than 64 million votes, compared with fewer than 60 million for Bolsonaro, a margin of nearly 4 percent.

In his video on Monday, Bolsonaro also said he was attempting to organize opposition among his congressional colleagues to the election results. His eight-year term as a senator expires January 31, 2027, which will also cause him to lose special jurisdiction at the country's Supreme Court.
news.summary: The United States will issue Flávio Bolsonaro a visa after he fled Brazil following his devastating loss to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday's election.

news.title: 'I looked at his ass': The truth about Trump's sudden fixation with other men's bodies, revealed by JAMES ROSEN
news.text:
Even by the loose standards of The Weave, as President Trump calls his speeches – those long, digressive cocktails of domestic and foreign policy, brilliant insights and schoolyard put-downs – the sheer awkwardness of That Moment in Ohio, for fans and critics alike, was jarring.

It was October 12 and the president was campaigning for Republican Senator Jon Husted in Youngstown: the Rust Belt community that once annually produced ten million tons of steel, a tough place for tough people. The 3,000 attendees who packed the Covelli Centre love their president for his toughness.

Husted is stout and fit with blandly symmetrical features. With his prominent forehead and chin, sleepy-eyed smile and thinning gray hair, Husted looks like the affable owner of a car dealership or dental practice. Forty years ago, he played cornerback at the University of Dayton, part of the Flyers' 1989 NCAA Division III championship team.

When he and the president met at Youngstown, they were not strangers. According to the online database maintained by Roll Call Factbase, Mr Trump had shared a stage with Husted, who has held elective office continuously since 2001, more than a dozen times over a decade, always acknowledging him by name. But Mr Trump had never said anything memorable about him – until this month.

In remarks at Vandalia-Butler High School in Vandalia, Ohio on October 3, Mr Trump disclosed that he had just learned of Husted's gridiron heroics. 'Nobody told me you were a great athlete,' the president said. 'Now I look at him… different.'

A half-hour later, the president prompted cheering: Hoo-STED! Hoo-STED! He thought the crowd gazed upon their junior senator in the same new light that he did: 'They know you're a good football player now… Otherwise they wouldn't be doing that. It's what happens when you're a football star.'

A football star! It was all the president could think about.

'He was an all-American,' Mr Trump told the audience forty minutes later. 

Nine days later, in Youngstown, Mr Trump decided to lean heavily into the football star business, raising it less than a minute into his remarks, professing amazement at how seldom Husted bragged about it. 'If I had his football record,' the president joked, 'they would have thought I was Jimmy Brown.'

His entire view of the senator had changed. 'He's, like, become a different man now,' Mr Trump said. But the truly jarring moment, the one that reverberated nationwide, came when he shared aloud the mechanics of this new sizing-up.

'I have to say,' the president began, adding 'I don't do this with men very often' before revealing: 'I started examining his body… up and down. I looked at his ass and I looked at the whole — '

Here the crowd, not knowing what else to do, began laughing.

' — and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands. He's got these, like, claws. And I got it. You are a great athlete! I didn't know that because he doesn't talk about that. Congratulations. Now they finally know. That was very good.'

No, that was very weird.

A search of the American Presidency Project, the online database of all the presidents' papers maintained by the University of California at Santa Barbara, finds, unsurprisingly, no other instance when a chief executive spoke or wrote the words I looked at his ass.

Indeed, the annals of the presidency record only two dozen uses of the phrase his ass – all from Mr Trump. Most referred to other people's asses being kicked, saved, fired, sued off, thrown in jail, gotten in gear or handed to them, but one cited the stated intention of an unnamed individual to 'break' Mr Trump's.

By the time he returned to Michigan on Sunday, President Trump acknowledged that his previous remarks about the senator's posterior amounted to 'my mistake.'

'In fun, I said I looked at his ass — and I've never done that with a man before, it's true. Off the record,' he continued before the assembled thousands, 'women, yes, men, no, okay?'

That yielded to a digression, almost as jaw-dropping, about the nearby hip-hop star who is, rather improbably, one of MAGA's biggest showbiz supporters.

'By the way, I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before: Nicki Minaj,' the chief executive said to audience laughter. 'That's hard to miss.'

Then The Weave wove back to Husted. 'While he's speaking… I'm examining his body. And I said, "His ass was like a big piece of muscle." The press went crazy the next day. They said, "What's with Trump? All he wants to do is talk about a man's ass." They didn't explain the whole football deal.'

Putting aside what good he thought discussion of Jon's Anatomy would do for the task at hand – persuading Ohio's Republican/MAGA voters to turn out at the polls on November 3 – we are left to wonder why a politician who has met countless athletes but never descended into such talk would feel compelled to do so now.

Of course, descriptions of the physical attractiveness of both men and women have long figured prominently in the president's rhetoric, most often preceded or capped by reference to the anointed individual as 'Central Casting,' the century-old Hollywood casting firm. Just four days after the first Husted Eruption, the president described Georgia's GOP gubernatorial candidate, Rick Jackson, as 'a very handsome, distinguished, beautiful-looking guy.'

As early as March 2016, when John Kasich and Marco Rubio were still competing for the Republican nomination, reporter Peter Alexander, then of NBC News, asked Mr Trump how parents should explain his profanity to children.

'Oh, you're so politically correct. You're so beautiful. Oh, look at you,' Mr Trump told Alexander. 'You've never heard a little bad — a little off language… Aren't you just a perfect young man.'

Perhaps most astonishing – anticipating the Husted Eruption – were Mr Trump's remarks in Latrobe, Pennsylvania, in the closing days of the 2024 cycle.

Leading with a tribute to Latrobe's most famous son, the late golf legend Arnold Palmer, the former president said he was determined to tell the 3,000 gathered at Arnold Palmer Regional Airport 'the real story of Arnold.'

'I love women,' Mr Trump said, 'but this guy — this is a guy that was all man… When he took showers with the other pros, they came out there, they said, "Oh my God, that's unbelievable."'

Mr Trump seemed to understand that his rhetoric had crossed some kind of line. 'I had to say it,' he professed, semi-apologizing. 'We have women that are highly sophisticated here. But they used to look at Arnold — this is bad — but he was really something special.'

Contacted by the Associated Press, Palmer's daughter Peg, then 68, chastised Mr Trump for a 'poor choice of approaches to remembering my father.'

So what on earth is going on? 

MAGA media personalities were quick to dismiss the prospect held out by Occam's Razor: namely, that the simplest explanation is usually the correct one.

'I can't imagine someone who is more beamingly heterosexual than Donald Trump,' declared my Newsmax colleague, radio and podcast host Rob Carson.

And the evidence – three marriages, five children, the self-described 'locker room talk,' and much else adduced to date – bears this out.

The proper lens for understanding President Trump's loquacity on other people's looks is not sexual but generational.

Though he has lost a step since 2024, Mr Trump, at 80, remains vigorous enough to crank up The Weave in different states each night, sometimes twice a day. Sometimes his antics, particularly his gift for cutting comedy, can conjure a younger vibe.

But he will always be a product of mid-century outer-borough New York, a time and place when a man could comment approvingly on the looks of other men – Cary Grant, say, or Jack Kennedy – without his sexuality called immediately into question. Gotham-based TV shows such as 'Batman' and 'The Odd Couple' depicted male co-occupancy without arousing snickers. None of it flies today.

It's the same generational heritage that leads the president to reference bygone names such as Jimmy Brown, to employ the New Yorker's testy coda, Ya understand? or to berate a female reporter for interjecting too frequently with Quiet, piggy.

As a veteran Washington reporter and an outer-borough New Yorker myself, one who came of age with Donald Trump as a daily staple of his media diet, I've believed since 2016 that more about the man is explicable by reference to his Big Apple origins than most people – especially his critics – have ever understood.

Ya understand?

James Rosen is chief Washington correspondent at Newsmax and the author, most recently, of Scalia: Supreme Court Years, 1986-2001.
news.summary: 'I have to say,' the president began, adding 'I don't do this with men very often' before revealing: 'I started examining his body… up and down. I looked at his ass and I looked at the whole.'

news.title: Nate Silver’s Midterm Predictions on ‘End of the Trump Era’ and AI
news.text: Election forecaster Nate Silver predicts that the 2026 midterms could mark the beginning of a post-Trump political era, while also offering an early test of voters' attitudes toward artificial intelligence and the data centers that power it. "If the election goes roughly as the polls say it will go, then in some ways, it would mark the end of the Trump era," Silver said on the Ezra Klein podcast Tuesday. Silver argued that a poor Republican performance would immediately shift political attention toward the 2028 presidential race and turn Trump into a "super lame duck" during the final two years of his term. "Maybe we're on the verge of something different," Silver said, citing generational turnover, Trump's approaching departure from office and the emergence of new political issues. The forecaster pointed to a steady decline in President Donald Trump's approval ratings because of the war in Iran, economic worries and higher gas prices. He noted voter fatigue after more than a decade of Trump dominating national politics. "He's been the dominant figure in American politics since whatever, mid-2015," Silver said. "That's a really long time." Do Democrats Retake the House and Senate? Silver gamed out a few scenarios—including one where the success predicted for Democrats fails to materialize. He said he can see a scenario where Democrats lose several of the closest Senate races, including James Talarico's race in Texas and Troy Jackson's in Maine. "Maybe pollsters and Democrats are getting their hopes up a little bit too high to think you could win in these R plus 12 states who have been R plus eight. Then yeah, but we just kind of reached the point where we ran out of like oxygen climbing up that big red hill, right?" he said. Several races have "a lot of outsized narrative importance," including Talarico's, along with Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan battle, Silver added. "You know, the possibility of Democrats being competitive in Texas, a sort of return of a religious left. Abdul El-Sayed is going to be seen as a very important test. He's actually not a DSA guy, but sort of a more left populist. ... It feels like there's going to be a lot of attention on how he specifically does." Silver identified another key question: whether moderate Democrats outperform more progressive candidates. He repeatedly highlighted candidate quality as a major factor in competitive Senate races and suggested November's results could influence the party's internal debate heading into 2028. "If El Sayed were to lose, then win or lose the Senate, that's a very bad narrative for progressives," he said. At the same time, Silver cautioned against reading too much into any single race, noting that broader political conditions remain more important than ideology alone. Klein asked Silver if it's possible that Trump doesn't really care whether the GOP holds the Senate, saying that he has made most of his policy changes through executive orders. "If winning the midterm means giving Republicans space from him and, you know, backing people he doesn't really like, yeah, then no" Silver said. AI Emerges as a Political Issue Silver suggested the election could provide an early indication of the potential backlash against artificial intelligence, particularly against the construction of data centers that support AI systems. "The two big sub-storylines of November 3 are one: how do progressives do relative to moderates?" Silver said. "But then, is there evidence of like an AI backlash from the state-by-state results?" He suggested analysts could eventually examine whether Republican candidates underperformed in areas where major data center projects were proposed or under construction. Silver also argued AI could become one of the defining issues of the next presidential election. "With AI looming too," he said, "it could be the biggest issue of 2028." The election forecaster added that the midterms could be remembered not simply as a referendum on Trump, but as a transition point. He described a political environment shaped by economic uncertainty, foreign policy tensions and rapid technological change. If Democrats perform as current polling suggests, Silver believes the election could accelerate a shift away from the political era Trump has dominated for more than a decade and toward a new debate over who leads both parties, and how the country responds to AI-driven change. "It's not quite clear to me how big an issue AI is in this election," Silver said. "I think maybe more than people assume." news.summary: Election forecaster Nate Silver predicts that the 2026 midterms could mark the onset of a post-Trump political era.

news.title: US midterms: 470 seats, $12 billion and one absent president
news.text: Washington: Americans go to the polls on November 3 for elections that will shape the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency - although the president himself will not be on any ballot.The “midterms,” held halfway through a president’s four-year term, decide control of Congress as well as governorships and thousands of state-level offices.A Democratic takeover of either chamber would constrain Trump’s agenda and bring greater congressional scrutiny of his administration; Republican victories would preserve the party’s control in Washington.Here is a look at the 2026 showdown by the numbers: House of Representatives435: Every seat in the House, the lower chamber of Congress, is contested every two years.218: The magic number for a majority in the 435-seat chamber.3: The net number of seats Democrats need to gain from the 2024 election result to take control. Republicans won a 220-215 majority then, although deaths, resignations and a party switch mean the current House stands at 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent and two vacancies..Trump promises Americans $5,000 if Republicans win Congress. For Republicans, that means a net loss of two seats is survivable. Three is not. Senate and the states35: Senate seats being contested - 33 in the normal six-year rotation plus special elections in Florida and Ohio.Republicans hold a 53-47 advantage in the 100-seat chamber, counting two independents who vote with the Democrats. Democrats therefore need a net gain of four seats to reach the 51 required for control; a 50-50 tie would be broken by Republican Vice President JD Vance.36: States electing governors, nearly three-quarters of the total.6,139: State legislative seats being regularly contested, across 88 of the country’s 99 state legislative chambers.What the polls say53-41 percent: The Democratic advantage over Republicans among registered voters asked which party’s congressional candidate they would support, in a PBS News/NPR/Marist poll conducted September 14-15.The same survey found Democrats ahead among independent voters by 57 percent to 32 percent.32-41 percent: The range of Trump’s approval rating in several major September surveys..Trump is getting the Republican Party he wants. But can he win in the midterms?. Reuters/Ipsos put him at 32 percent among US adults, the lowest of his political career, while Marist recorded 39 percent and NBC News 41 percent among registered voters. The surveys use different methodologies and populations, so the figures are not directly comparable - but none suggests an abundance of presidential coattails.55 percent: Registered voters who told NBC News that Trump’s policies had hurt the economy, against 26 percent who said they had helped it. Money, money, moneyAbout $12 billion: The amount expected to be spent advertising on the 2025-26 election cycle.Ad-tracking company AdImpact forecasts $11.6 billion, exceeding both the previous midterm record of $8.9 billion in 2022 and even the 2024 presidential cycle.Kinetiq Political Insights’ latest estimate is slightly higher at $11.96 billion, with a projected range of $11.5 billion to $12.5 billion.$330 million: Advertising spending in the California governor’s primary alone, according to AdImpact - making the preliminary contest to choose November’s candidates the most expensive gubernatorial race on record.And that was merely the warm-up. For the trivia file2,497: Candidates who ran in US congressional primaries this year, the most in any election cycle since at least 2014. An extraordinary 2,232 of them were chasing House seats.44: House races on November 3 that are rematches between the same major-party candidates who fought for the seat in 2024.Broaden the search to state and local contests and there are 474 electoral rematches nationwide - proving that in American politics, as in Hollywood, there is rarely any objection to a sequel.

news.title: Cassidy Hutchinson avoids indictment after DOJ effort to charge her over Jan. 6 testimony fails: sources
news.text: A federal grand jury in Washington, D.C., declined to indict former Trump White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson after the Justice Department sought criminal charges over statements she made to Congress in 2022, two sources confirmed to Fox News Digital. The Justice Department had sought to indict Hutchinson over allegations that she lied to the House committee investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot, but the effort failed Tuesday, according to the sources. It remains unclear whether federal prosecutors will make another attempt to secure an indictment. During a nationally televised hearing in June 2022, Hutchinson testified about Trump's actions on Jan. 6, including an account she said she heard from another White House official about the president's reaction after being told he could not travel to the Capitol. Her account of an alleged confrontation inside the presidential vehicle was subsequently disputed by other individuals familiar with the events. At the time, a source familiar with the matter said additional evidence could be presented to the grand jury as soon as the following week and that no final decisions had been made about whether the investigation would result in criminal charges. The New York Post also reported that the Justice Department was investigating Hutchinson over possible false statements to Congress. DOJ OPENS INVESTIGATION INTO TRUMP ALLY COREY LEWANDOWSKI The grand jury's decision not to indict Hutchinson does not establish whether her congressional testimony was truthful or false. Hutchinson has previously maintained that she stands by her testimony. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to the Justice Department, Rep. news.title: Former Miss Switzerland accuses Donald Trump of rape
news.text:
Donald Trump has been accused of rape by a model and former Miss Switzerland in a report produced by the Democratic Party.

Beatrice Keul, who shortly before the 2024 election claimed the president had groped her in November 1993, has now alleged that Mr Trump also raped her during that incident.

The report, released Monday, detailed an investigation by US House Democrats into Mr Trump’s alleged connections to Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.

The White House denied the report’s allegations, with a spokesman describing the claims as “a desperate attempt by crazed Democrats to distract Americans from the surging Republican momentum driven by President Trump’s historic achievements”.

During interviews with Democratic committee staffers “over several weeks”, Ms Keul said she met Mr Trump when she was 24 at a press event for a pageant at New York’s Plaza Hotel, which he owned at the time.

According to Ms Keul, Mr Trump allegedly promised that he would arrange a visa for her and said he could ensure that she got accepted into New York University (NYU). “I will take care of you,” he told her, according to the claims in the report.

After Mr Trump stepped away from their conversation, Ms Keul said she was immediately approached by Epstein, who described himself as “Don’s best friend” and invited her to a party at Mar-a-Lago.

“We organise many parties with Don,” Epstein apparently told her. Mr Trump says that he ended his friendship with Epstein long before there were suspicions of any criminal wrongdoing and has repeatedly described him as a “creep” whom he kicked out of his Mar-a-Lago club.

According to the Democrats’ report, a representative for Mr Trump later allegedly invited Ms Keul to meet the future president upstairs at the Plaza Hotel.

“Upon entering, Trump reportedly grabbed Keul from behind and forcibly raped her; in the process, tearing her dress and causing bleeding and bruising on multiple parts of her body,” the report claimed.

“Keul described the rape as ‘brutal,’” the report added. Following the alleged assault, Ms Keul claimed that Mr Trump “sat her on the edge of the bed, repeated his promises to arrange for a visa and NYU admission, and made her promise she would keep quiet, saying, ‘[T]he show must go on.’”

In Ms Keul’s original claims in October 2024, she accused Mr Trump of groping her at the Plaza Hotel in 1993.

“He kissed me on the lips and on the neck. He tried to lift my dress. He was grabbing and touching my body everywhere he could,” she told The Daily Mail.

But she said things did not go further. “I tried everything I could. Finally, I said ‘let’s talk first’ or something like that, then he slowed down,” she said.

The 6ft 1in ex-model suggested it was her size that “saved her” from the alleged attack from escalating.

The newspaper also reported that a longtime friend said Ms Keul “first told him her story of Trump’s unwanted sexual advances 20 years ago, and that her telling of the incident has not changed in the intervening years.”

Allegations dismissed as ‘fake’

At the time, Karoline Leavitt, then press secretary to Mr Trump, described the allegations as “fake”.

A White House spokesman said Mr Trump had been “fully exonerated of anything related to Epstein.”

“This ‘report’ is nothing more than a desperate attempt by crazed Democrats to distract Americans from the surging Republican momentum driven by President Trump’s historic achievements,” they said.

The newly released report summarises the accounts of four other women who have accused Mr Trump of rape or sexual assault.

It also claims that Mr Trump, Epstein and others used the pageant at the Plaza Hotel as a “‘hunting ground’ to prey on vulnerable young women and girls.”

“Five women have directly accused Trump of rape or sexual assault in Epstein’s company or presence; others have indicated that Epstein or Maxwell attempted to traffic them to Trump,” Jamie Raskin, the committee’s ranking member, said in a statement alongside the release of the report.

“Trump’s Justice Department appears to be covering up these crimes to protect the President,” he added.

The report landed just a week before the US midterm elections. Mr Trump’s handling of the Epstein files – along with inflation and rising energy prices caused by his war with Iran – has hamstrung Republican candidates even though the US president is not on the ballot.
news.summary: Donald Trump has been accused of rape by a model and former Miss Switzerland in a report produced by the Democratic Party.
news.author: David Apinga

news.title: Trump makes last-minute push to keep Texas in Republican hands with third trip
news.text: President Donald Trump was in Texas for the third time in a month on Tuesday in a last-minute push to block Democrats from notching their first statewide election victory in more than three decades in next week's midterm elections.Trump was in Corpus Christi and will later travel to Lubbock to boost Republican Ken Paxton’s competitive U.S. Senate campaign against Democrat James Talarico. Not ceding the stage to the presidential spotlight, Talarico was in Amarillo, where he assailed a “broken, corrupt” political system. Like Trump and Paxton, he'll later appear in Lubbock.Democrat Gina Hinojosa is also waging a spirited campaign against GOP Gov. Greg Abbott, who is seeking his fourth term.The president leaned into cultural issues to portray Talarico as too liberal for Texas. And as Trump's war in Iran spikes gas prices and adds pressure on Republican candidates across the U.S., he sought to highlight an earlier military operation in Venezuela. Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefly appeared on stage with Trump, who used the trip in part to highlight the arrangement made with Venezuela to process more of its crude oil in Texas refineries.“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history,” Trump said in Corpus Christi.Trump is entering the final week of his last midterms in a frenzied push to shore up Republican strongholds against unusually competitive Democratic candidates. Beyond Texas, he swung through Mississippi, Michigan, Georgia, Florida and Iowa over the past week, and his next stops are Ohio, South Carolina, Florida, Kansas and Iowa again.He won all of these states in 2024.RELATED STORY | Trump faces hecklers while making high-profile Texas campaign pushTexas tests Trump's sway over the GOPThe campaign marathon is a bet that while Trump is broadly unpopular, he still holds sway over the GOP's most loyal voters — a bloc whose participation in the elections will be critical.The strategy is facing its fiercest test in Texas, where Talarico has capitalized on the difficult political environment for Republicans and Paxton's history of ethical and legal problems.Trump argued that Paxton was a “good man” and Elon Musk, the world's richest man, has joined Trump's effort to stop Talarico's advance.“Talarico is lunatic left,” Musk wrote on his social media platform, X, to his 241 million followers, part of a drumbeat of attacks he’s posted against the candidate in the race’s final days.Musk has headquartered Tesla and SpaceX, as well as himself, in Texas, and is so set on ensuring Republicans hold control of his adopted state that he appears to have sunk at least $158 million into defeating Talarico. Musk gave that much to the Senate Leadership Fund, which then gave the same amount to the Texas PAC, the largest contributor to Paxton’s campaign.That’s helped make the race one of the most expensive in the country, with over $563 million being spent on advertising between the primary and general elections, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact.While Musk’s investment is a challenge for Talarico, it also falls right into the Democratic campaign’s central message. At every stop, Talarico has argued that, for too long, the wealthy and their donations have corrupted politics, and that this corruption has fueled the affordability crisis.Talarico has begun naming Musk in his stump speeches. Paxton tends not to discuss him.That parallels the Texas governor's race.Hinojosa has sued to be able to view communications between Musk and Abbott, arguing that their relationship evinces how cozy her opponent is with the ultra-wealthy in Texas.On Monday, a judge ruled that Hinojosa, given her position as a state representative, must be able to review over 1,000 unredacted pages by Thursday.RELATED STORY | Trump heads to Mississippi as more red states enter the midterm conversation with 8 days to goRubio's visit previews GOP's potential 2028 contestAs the midterms reach the final stretch, the early stages of the next campaign are already surfacing.Rubio, who also serves as Trump’s national security adviser, is hitting the road with Trump for the first time as the president barnstorms the country.A State Department official said Rubio is traveling with Trump in his capacity as national security advisor and not secretary of state.The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the travel plans, said Rubio “needs time with the president on all kinds of issues” and that “being on the plane with him gives him a chance to talk to him about these items.”Rubio previously ran for president in 2016 and is considered a top prospect in 2028. He has not said whether he will run, and his political activities have been limited since becoming secretary of state.He appeared on stage with Trump briefly in Corpus Christi — and only after Trump repeatedly called on him to come forward.“It’s an honor to work for the greatest country in the world, for the greatest president in the history of the United States of America,” he said before exiting.Another top Republican 2028 contender, Vice President JD Vance, has been more active on the campaign trail, stopping in Michigan on Tuesday, where he called the Senate race between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed a “clash of competing visions.”Ahead of his trip, Vance echoed Trump's concerns about another critical Senate race in Alaska. The president said last week that he ordered the Department of Justice to file a lawsuit to block certification of the race there if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses. Trump has long complained about the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan, who Republicans fear could siphon away votes from the incumbent.“When you put a person on the ballot explicitly to try to confuse voters, I think that’s the definition of electoral fraud and I don’t think we should endorse it,” Vance said when asked why voters can’t tell the Dan Sullivans apart.Alaska voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” will not have a party affiliation.Alaska’s Republican election officials determined the other Sullivan’s campaign was an attempt to “mislead” voters and wanted him removed from the ballot. But both a state court and Alaska’s Supreme Court disagreed and kept the second Sullivan on the ballot.In California, Xavier Becerra, a Democrat running for governor, urged voters to reject a voter ID ballot measure, which he said would make it harder for people to vote.“We want democracy not just to shine, but be so resilient and so strong that Donald Trump cannot knock California down,” Becerra said in San Francisco.For all the headwinds confronting Republicans, Speaker Mike Johnson sought to project confidence as he joined Rep. Mike Lawler of New York, one of the House's most vulnerable incumbents.“I think we are due for a great election,” Johnson said.
news.summary: President Trump was in Texas for a third time Tuesday, seeking to shore up Republican strongholds against unusually competitive Democratic candidates in this year's elections.
news.author: AP via Scripps News Group

news.title: Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro flees to US after election loss
news.text: BRASILÍA — Defeated right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro left Brazil and is traveling to the United States despite a court order banning him from exiting the country, US media reported Tuesday.The son of jailed ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro lost the presidential election Sunday to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and refused to concede defeat.The right-wing senator on Monday said a Supreme Court justice had ordered him to hand over his passports. Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering, and with his election loss is also set to lose parliamentary immunity.The 45-year-old was traveling to Florida, CNN reported, citing an anonymous official source. Other US media confirmed he was heading to the country.The US State Department said Tuesday it would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family, without confirming his travel plans.A police source told AFP that the senator's Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been canceled, adding that 'there is no formal record of Flavio Bolsonaro leaving the country.'But he has held Italian nationality since 2023, according to an Italian parliamentary document seen by AFP.Bolsonaro's campaign manager Rogerio Marinho expressed shock over reports that the defeated candidate had fled Brazil.'We still don't have any news about his whereabouts,' he told reporters Tuesday in Brasilia.'I received a text message from him this morning, where he said he would let some time pass today and then would talk with us, and that was it,' Marinho said.'That was the only communication we had.''Shameful'Lula called fleeing the country a 'shameful' act.'A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide. The act of leaving Brazil is shameful,' he remarked in Brasilia during his 81st birthday celebration.Bolsonaro said Monday that the ban on his exit from Brazil amounted to a scare tactic.'I never had any intention of leaving the country,' he said in a video posted on Instagram.US President Donald Trump, a close ally of Jair Bolsonaro, on Monday said Brazil's elections were 'rigged' following the defeat of Bolsonaro junior.Flavio's brother Eduardo, a US-based former lawmaker, maintains close ties with the White House.Last week, he told a US podcast that Flavio Bolsonaro should leave Brazil in the event of electoral defeat, given the active probes into his activities.In his Monday statement, Lula's challenger also said he would lead the opposition to the leftist government.Following Lula's victory with 51.8 percent of the vote, Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the result, citing the decision to extend polling hours over transportation difficulties that prevented some citizens from voting.Lula had requested the extension, as had Bolsonaro over bad weather in parts of the country.In his father's footstepsAll bets were on a Bolsonaro win after he came out on top in the first round of elections earlier this month.He campaigned on a pledge to liberate his father, who is under house arrest for coup-plotting after his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022.Jair Bolsonaro never conceded defeat and left the country on the eve of his rival's inauguration, only returning to Brazil three months later.Separately on Tuesday, the Supreme Court ordered police to investigate alleged foreign funding of Flavio Bolsonaro's campaign and other interference from abroad such as social media 'manipulation.'Lula's campaign complained about election interference by Meta, the parent company of WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, claiming 'algorithmic manipulation.'Meta denies taking any actions to favor one side in the election, but previously said that some of Lula's campaign ads had been mistakenly deactivated due to technical errors.
news.author: Agence France-Presse

news.title: U.S. to give visa to Brazilian election loser Bolsonaro
news.text: U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration plans to issue visas to defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro and his family, a senior State Department official announced, confirming multiple reports that the senator fled his country following his loss.Bolsonaro is en route to the U.S. and is likely to land in either Dallas or Miami, Folha de S.Paulo reported earlier in the day. The visas will allow Bolsonaro and his family to enter the U.S., according to the State Department official.Bolsonaro, who is facing multiple criminal investigations in Brazil, was ordered to surrender his passports to Federal Police on Tuesday but failed to do so, according to a police official familiar with the situation. Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, whom the Bolsonaro family has long accused of political persecution, demanded he turn over the documents amid concerns the senator posed a flight risk.
news.summary: The defeated presidential candidate is reportedly en route to the U.S. following his loss to incumbent Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.

news.title: Hackers target US FEC systems, shutting down electronic filing just days before midterm elections
news.text:
The U.S. Federal Election Commission (FEC) was forced to temporarily shut down its web-facing services and electronic filing system following a targeted hacking attempt.

In a statement, the FEC said that, "at this time, the FEC’s electronic filing system is currently offline and our IT staff are actively working to restore service."

The FEC, which tracks the spending of candidates and political committees, said that users could still search the website for past reports while declining to further comment on the outage.

The outage which began late Monday evening, just one week before the November 3 midterm elections has disrupted the ability of political committees, candidates, and super PACs to submit mandatory 24-hour and 48-hour spending reports.

The agency's electronic reporting gateway remains offline while IT staff work to restore services. While the public and media can still search historical archives for past disclosures, live campaign finance transparency has taken an immediate hit.

Federal officials and cybersecurity experts emphasize that the FEC does not administer actual elections or ballot-casting systems.

As reported, the hack will have no direct effect on voters' ability to cast ballots on November 3.

Campaign finance compliance experts note that a shutdown of this nature during the final, high-spending sprint of a midterm cycle is unprecedented.

Political groups are currently blocked from logging late-stage independent expenditures and advertising buys, temporarily reducing real-time public oversight.

The hacking attempts come a week before the midterm elections, which will determine whether President Donald Trump's Republicans maintain their majorities in Congress for the next two years.

The FEC does not play a role in administering US elections and the outage should have no effect on voters' ability to cast ballots.

The outage prevents organizations from filing the FEC's 24-hour and 48-hour spending reports, which show how much political groups and others are spending on specific races.

"I’ve never seen this in 26 years," said Steven Mele, a partner at political finance compliance firm MBA Consulting Group. "The result is there will be less disclosure on the elections” until it’s fixed.

Federal cybersecurity entities, including the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the FBI, have been monitoring the digital landscape, though a formal attribution for the breach attempt has not yet been publicly released.
news.author: Hafsa Naeem Baig

news.title: Trump’s energy secretary said president is about ‘driving energy prices down’ as Iran war continues to keep them high
news.text:
Energy Secretary Chris Wright defended the Trump administration’s economic record during a Tuesday appearance on Fox News, arguing that President Donald Trump was focused on lowering energy costs despite high gas prices driven by the Iran war.

Appearing on Fox News’s “America Reports,” Wright faced questioning from anchor John Roberts regarding elevated fuel costs. 

“Let’s talk about gas prices,” Roberts said. “They are still naggingly high. The president has been saying since March that they’re going to come down. They haven’t. There’s no relief in sight and certainly none expected before November 3rd, so what do you tell consumers?”

An on-screen display showed the national average for regular gasoline standing at $4.27 per gallon, compared to $3.05 a year ago and $4.48 a month prior.

Wright acknowledged the financial effect of foreign policy decisions. 

“Making sure that Iran doesn’t get a nuclear weapon absolutely has come at a cost,” he said. “But gasoline prices peaked several weeks ago. They have been slowly coming down. … We want to see it lower. They will go lower — conflict-related.”

Wright added: “The difference is, with Democrat energy policies, they never go away. Republican policies are about energy addition. President Trump’s about driving energy prices down. But yes, he is ending Iran’s nuclear program, and that’s causing a temporary elevation of prices. Very unfortunate that it’s around election time, but he’s governing for the long term.”

Co-anchor Sandra Smith questioned Wright on the potential political fallout.

“Seven days out from the midterm elections, how much of a political liability do you think these high energy prices are for the Republican Party?” Smith said. 

Wright acknowledged the voter frustration.

“People are clearly upset about higher energy prices,” Wright said. “Energy is fundamental to people’s lives. We’ve had these [Democratic] policies that have just needlessly driven up energy prices. The Trump administration has been all about doing exactly the opposite.” 

During the exchange, network graphics showed diesel fuel was averaging $6.35 per gallon, up from $3.66 last year.

Roberts pushed back on the idea of long-term relief. 

“Although if the president does come back to kinetic activity in Iran, I’m sure the prices will go back up again, even though they’ve come down,” he said. 

The exchange comes as nationwide gas prices remain higher than during the Biden administration, according to recent federal data. 

During Trump’s second term, Americans have paid an average of $3.74 for a gallon of unleaded gas, compared to $3.69 under Joe Biden, according to Federal Reserve price tracking. Earlier this month, fuel tracker Patrick De Haan noted on social media that prices had exceeded $4 per gallon for 158 days in 2026 — more than any previous year.

At the start of 2026, unleaded fuel averaged less than $3 per gallon before the war in Iran began in late February. Slowed oil shipping drove average gas prices above $4 per gallon in March, peaking at $4.65 in May before rebounding to $4.48 by September.

A New York Times/Siena University poll found that 73 percent of voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of gas prices. 

Speaking at a rally last week, Trump said he “doesn’t give a damn” that Americans are paying more for gas, and that the U.S. was making “hundreds of billions of dollars” on oil because of the Iran War.

Voters across the country have expressed growing concern over inflation.

“Groceries are just like kind of out of control,” Iowa farmer Bethany Lnenicka, a three-time Trump voter, said. “It seems like everything is going up. It’s just one thing and the next week it’s another thing. It’s just insane. And of course your income doesn’t go up.”

To mitigate rising costs, the administration has taken regulatory measures in recent months, including increasing domestic diesel production, granting tax breaks on commercial diesel fuel and temporarily rolling back environmental rules on select gasoline blends.
news.summary: National fuel costs remain high as the Trump administration ties elevated prices to efforts to block Iran’s nuclear program
news.author: Jasmine Fernández
